AHT-FNH.name: Badshot Lea Long Barrow
AHT-FNH.text: Your train passes near the site of Badshot Lea Long Barrow, on the train's {side}, an earthen burial mound probably built more than 5,000 years ago, the only long barrow known in Surrey. Little was left by 1936, when it was excavated because a chalk quarry was about to swallow the rest.

BTY-FNH.name: William Cobbett pub, Farnham
BTY-FNH.text: Your train passes near the William Cobbett pub in Farnham, on the train's {side}, once the Jolly Farmer, where the radical writer and MP William Cobbett was born in 1763. It was renamed after him.

AON-BTY.name: St Lawrence's Church, Alton
AON-BTY.text: Your train passes near St Lawrence's Church in Alton, on the train's {side}, probably begun not long after 1066. On December 13th 1643, in the Civil War, Royalist soldiers made their last stand in it before Parliament's troops broke through the west door.

AHT-ASH.name: Holy Trinity Church, Aldershot
AHT-ASH.text: Your train passes near Holy Trinity Church in Aldershot, on the train's {side}, built between 1875 and 1878, the first new church in a town that had grown fast once the Army arrived in the 1850s.

AHV-FML.name: Frimley Green Windmill
AHV-FML.text: Your train passes near Frimley Green Windmill, on the train's {side}, a brick tower mill first recorded in 1784. From 1803 it belonged to the Royal Military College at Sandhurst; it stopped work by 1870 and became a house in 1914.

CAM-FML.name: Staff College, Camberley
CAM-FML.text: Your train passes near the old Staff College at Camberley, on the train's {side}, which trained the Army's staff officers until 1997. It grew out of a college opened in High Wycombe in 1799.

BAG-CAM.name: Camberley Obelisk
BAG-CAM.text: Your train passes near the Camberley Obelisk, on the train's {side}, which is really a square brick tower, built on a wooded hill in about 1765 to 1770 by the merchant John Norris. It once stood much taller.

ACT-BAG.name: Bagshot Park
ACT-BAG.text: Your train passes along Bagshot Park, on the train's {side}, a royal home whose house was built in 1879 for Prince Arthur, Duke of Connaught. An earlier lodge here was rebuilt for Charles I by Inigo Jones.

ACT-MAO.name: Englemere House
ACT-MAO.text: Your train passes near Englemere House, on the train's {side}, an Italianate house of about 1815 that was the home of Field Marshal Lord Roberts from 1903 until his death in 1914.

BCE-MAO.name: RAF Staff College, Bracknell
BCE-MAO.text: Your train passes near the former RAF Staff College at Bracknell, on the train's {side}, where the Royal Air Force trained its staff officers from 1945 to 1997, in a Victorian house called Ramslade House.

BCE-WKM.name: Ranelagh School
BCE-WKM.text: Your train passes near Ranelagh School in Bracknell, on the train's {side}, a Church of England school founded by Lord Ranelagh in 1709.

ACT-SNG.name: Charters House
ACT-SNG.text: Your train passes near Charters, on the train's {side}, an Art Deco house built in 1938 for the industrialist Frank Parkinson. His guests included Winston Churchill and the Duke and Duchess of Windsor.

LNG-SNG.name: Bromhall Priory
LNG-SNG.text: Your train passes near the site of Bromhall Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of Benedictine nuns from 1200. The Pope suppressed it in 1524, and its lands went to St John's College, Cambridge.

LNG-VIR.name: Longcross Studios
LNG-VIR.text: Your train passes near Longcross Studios, on the train's {side}, opened in 2006 where military vehicles were tested from 1942 to 2005 and Chobham armour was developed. The James Bond film Skyfall was made here.

EGH-VIR.name: Holloway Sanatorium
EGH-VIR.text: Your train passes near the old Holloway Sanatorium, on the train's {side}, built between 1873 and 1885 for the philanthropist Thomas Holloway to treat people with temporary mental illness. Pevsner called it and its sister, Royal Holloway College, the summit of High Victorian design; it is now homes.

CHY-VIR.name: St Ann's Hill
CHY-VIR.text: Your train passes near St Ann's Hill, on the train's {side}, the highest point in Chertsey. Its summit was a key viewing point for the survey of the 1780s that linked the Greenwich and Paris observatories by a chain of triangles.

ASN-CHY.name: Chertsey Abbey
ASN-CHY.text: Your train passes near the site of Chertsey Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 666 by Saint Erkenwald. King Henry VI was buried here before his body was moved to St George's Chapel, Windsor.

ASN-WYB.name: Coxes Lock
ASN-WYB.text: Your train passes near Coxes Lock on the Wey Navigation, on the train's {side}, built between 1651 and 1653. Its mill pond is the biggest on the navigation, and its old mill buildings are now flats.

BFN-WYB.name: Concorde G-BBDG, Brooklands Museum
BFN-WYB.text: Your train passes near Brooklands Museum, on the train's {side}, home to Concorde G-BBDG, built for testing before the planes carried passengers. It first flew in February 1974, last flew on Christmas Eve 1981, and came here by road in 2003.

BFN-WBY.name: Brooklands
BFN-WBY.text: Your train passes near Brooklands, on the train's {side}, opened in 1907 as the world's first purpose-built banked motor racing circuit, and one of Britain's first airfields. Its last race was in August 1939.

WBY-WOK.name: Shah Jahan Mosque
WBY-WOK.text: Your train passes near the Shah Jahan Mosque in Woking, on the train's {side}, the first purpose-built mosque in the United Kingdom, finished in 1889. A ship's captain was brought in to take the bearings that line it up with Mecca.

BKO-WOK.name: Brookwood Cemetery
BKO-WOK.text: Your train passes Brookwood Cemetery, on the train's {side}, the largest in the United Kingdom, opened in 1854 for London's dead. Coffins and mourners came out from a special station beside Waterloo, on a branch line into the cemetery.

WOK-WPL.name: Smart's and Prey Heaths
WOK-WPL.text: Your train passes near Smart's and Prey Heaths, on the train's {side}, damp heaths of ling and purple moor-grass where two kinds of sundew, small plants that catch insects, grow.

GLD-WPL.name: Guildford Cathedral
GLD-WPL.text: Your train passes near Guildford Cathedral, on the train's {side}, on top of Stag Hill. Designed by Edward Maufe and built between 1936 and 1961, it was the last Church of England cathedral to be consecrated on a new site.

FNC-GLD.name: St Catherine's Chapel, Guildford
FNC-GLD.text: Your train passes near the ruined chapel on St Catherine's Hill, on the train's {side}, built early in the 14th century; the railway runs through a tunnel under the hill. J. M. W. Turner drew the hill and chapel, and in 2020 work on the line uncovered a small sandstone cave with carved niches, thought to be a medieval shrine.

FNC-GOD.name: Charterhouse School
FNC-GOD.text: Your train passes near Charterhouse, on the train's {side}, a school founded by Thomas Sutton in 1611 on the site of a Carthusian monastery in London. It moved here in 1872, to a hilltop site just outside Godalming.

GOD-MLF.name: The Pepperpot, Godalming
GOD-MLF.text: Your train passes near the Pepperpot in Godalming High Street, on the train's {side}, a little market hall with a clock tower and cupola, finished in 1814. Markets were held under its arches, and the room upstairs housed the town's museum from 1921 to 1987.

MLF-WTY.name: Tigbourne Court
MLF-WTY.text: Your train passes near Tigbourne Court, on the train's {side}, a country house by Edwin Lutyens, finished in 1901 and called "probably his best" building. Edgar Horne, who had it built, never moved in, and it was let to the fraudster Whitaker Wright.

HSL-WTY.name: Haslemere Educational Museum
HSL-WTY.text: Your train passes near Haslemere Educational Museum, on the train's {side}, founded in 1888 by the surgeon Sir Jonathan Hutchinson for his natural history collection. It holds nearly half a million specimens, artefacts, papers and images, among them the mummy of Pa-Er-Abu, thought to have been an Egyptian priest.

HSL-LIP.name: Haslemere
HSL-LIP.text: Your train passes near Haslemere, on the train's {side}, thought to have begun as a planned town in the 12th century, with a market charter from 1221. The Dolmetsch Early Music Festival was founded here in 1925, and at the west end of Shottermill, in the same parish, Surrey, Hampshire and West Sussex meet.

LIP-LIS.name: Liss Riverside Railway Walk North
LIP-LIS.text: Your train passes near Liss Riverside Railway Walk, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve whose footpath runs through willow and alder woodland along the route of the Longmoor Military Railway, from Liss to Liss Forest.

LIS-PTR.name: Statue of William III, Petersfield
LIS-PTR.text: Your train passes near the statue of William III in Petersfield's square, on the train's {side}, a lead figure of the king as a Roman senator on horseback, made in about 1757 and once gilded. It first stood at the entrance to Petersfield House and was moved to the square when the house was pulled down in the 1790s.

PTR-RLN.name: St Hubert's Church, Idsworth
PTR-RLN.text: Your train passes near St Hubert's Church at Idsworth, on the train's {side}, the only place of worship of an isolated hamlet in the South Downs, with medieval paintings on its north wall and around the east window. The diocese calls it "the little church in the field".

HAV-RLN.name: Rowland's Castle
HAV-RLN.text: Your train passes the remains of Rowland's Castle, on the train's {side}, a motte-and-bailey castle built at some time between 1066 and 1189, where Henry II spent several days hunting. The railway and quarrying damaged the site in the 19th century, and only earthworks and a few bits of wall are left.

BDH-HAV.name: Havant
BDH-HAV.text: Your train passes near the middle of Havant, on the train's {side}, once home to the leading parchment works in southern England, which closed in 1936. The Treaty of Versailles was written on Havant parchment.

BDH-CSA.name: The Elms, Bedhampton
BDH-CSA.text: Your train passes near The Elms in Old Bedhampton, on the train's {side}, a 17th-century house given a Gothic Revival makeover in the 18th. Its owner, Sir Theophilus Lee, invited his relative the Duke of Wellington to dine here, and had a room made in his honour.

BDH-HLS.name: Portsmouth Airport
BDH-HLS.text: Your train passes the site of Portsmouth Airport, on the train's {side}, opened in 1932 with three grass runways between Hilsea and Langstone Harbour. From here ran the first air ferry in the south of England, to Ryde on the Isle of Wight; the last flight left on December 31st 1973.

HAV-WBL.name: Warblington Castle
HAV-WBL.text: Your train passes near Warblington Castle, on the train's {side}, a moated manor built between 1515 and 1525 for Margaret Pole, Countess of Salisbury. Most of it was destroyed in the Civil War, and only a gate tower, part of a wall and a gateway still stand.

EMS-WBL.name: Emsworth
EMS-WBL.text: Your train passes near Emsworth, on the train's {side}, at the head of an arm of Chichester Harbour, with a basin that fills at high tide and can be emptied through a sluice. The River Ems is named after the town, not the other way round: the chronicler Raphael Holinshed gave it the name in the 16th century.

EMS-SOB.name: Brook Meadow
EMS-SOB.text: Your train passes near Brook Meadow, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of grassland and woodland between two streams on the edge of Emsworth, looked after by volunteers. Its wildlife includes water voles.

NUT-SOB.name: Southbourne
NUT-SOB.text: Your train passes near Southbourne, on the train's {side}, a village that began in 1876, when its church of St John was consecrated. It sits in the western corner of West Sussex, with the Hampshire border just to the west.

BOH-NUT.name: Nutbourne
BOH-NUT.text: Your train passes near Nutbourne, on the train's {side}, a village at the northern tip of Thorney Channel, an inlet of Chichester Harbour. Its name probably comes from the South Saxons' hnutu burna, the stream overhung by nut trees.

BOH-FSB.name: Fishbourne Roman Palace
BOH-FSB.text: Your train passes near Fishbourne Roman Palace, on the train's {side}, the largest known Roman home north of the Alps, built around AD 75. Its mosaics include the Dolphin mosaic, and it burnt down in about 270, after which it was abandoned.

CCH-FSB.name: Chichester Cathedral
CCH-FSB.text: Your train passes near Chichester Cathedral, on the train's {side}, founded in 1075. It is the only medieval cathedral in England with a bell tower standing apart from the church, and its spire is the only one of a medieval English cathedral that can be seen from the sea.

BAA-CCH.name: Chichester Cross
BAA-CCH.text: Your train passes near Chichester Cross, on the train's {side}, an elaborate stone market cross about 50 feet tall, where the city's four main streets meet. Its inscription says Bishop Edward Story built it, so that poor people would have somewhere to sell their wares.

BAA-BOG.name: Bognor Regis
BAA-BOG.text: Your train passes near Bognor Regis, on the train's {side}, a resort laid out by Sir Richard Hotham in the late 18th century on an empty stretch of coast. King George V spent three months recovering here in 1929, and the town was given the name "Regis" later that year.

BAA-FOD.name: John Baker's Mill, Barnham
BAA-FOD.text: Your train passes near John Baker's Mill at Barnham, on the train's {side}, a flint and stone tower windmill built in 1829. It was worked by wind until the early 1920s and by engine until 1963.

FOD-LIT.name: St Mary Magdalene's Church, Tortington
FOD-LIT.text: Your train passes near St Mary Magdalene's Church at Tortington, on the train's {side}, founded in the 12th century and little changed since. Its chancel arch and doorway are carved with rare beakhead figures, described as "grotesque, boggle-eyed monsters".

ARU-FOD.name: Slayer's Slab, Lyminster
ARU-FOD.text: Your train passes near Lyminster church, on the train's {side}, home of the Slayer's Slab, a medieval gravestone with a cross on it and no name. Legend says it marks the grave of the man who killed the Knucker, the dragon of the nearby knuckerhole.

ANG-FOD.name: St Nicholas Church, Poling
ANG-FOD.text: Your train passes near St Nicholas Church at Poling, on the train's {side}, a flint church whose nave dates from Saxon times. A Saxon window found in its north wall in 1917 still has part of its original wooden shutter.

ANG-GBS.name: St Mary's Church, Goring-by-Sea
ANG-GBS.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at Goring-by-Sea, on the train's {side}, a Norman church given its present Gothic Revival look by Decimus Burton in 1837. Inside is a mural painted in 1954 by the German artist Hans Feibusch, which caused controversy at the time.

DUR-GBS.name: English Martyrs' Church, Goring-by-Sea
DUR-GBS.text: Your train passes near English Martyrs' Church in Goring-by-Sea, on the train's {side}, whose ceiling is a copy of Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted by hand by the sign-painter Gary Bevans between 1987 and 1993. The church is the same width as the Sistine Chapel, and a little shorter.

DUR-WWO.name: West Tarring
DUR-WWO.text: Your train passes near West Tarring, on the train's {side}, a village given to the archbishops of Canterbury in the 10th century, with a 13th-century Archbishop's Palace. Tradition says Thomas Becket visited, and it had a much-visited fig garden from 1745 or earlier.

WRH-WWO.name: Teville Stream
WRH-WWO.text: Your train passes near the Teville Stream, on the train's {side}, which rises at allotments in Tarring and runs through Worthing to the sea. It was once tidal and much wider; now it runs in culverts for much of its length.

EWR-WRH.name: Beach House, Worthing
EWR-WRH.text: Your train passes near Beach House in Worthing, on the train's {side}, a Regency villa built in 1820. King Edward VII stayed here several times between 1907 and 1910, and in 1936 it took in children from the Basque country, fleeing the Spanish Civil War.

EWR-LAC.name: Lancing Carriage Works
EWR-LAC.text: Your train passes the site of Lancing Carriage Works, on the train's {side}, where railway carriages and wagons were built and repaired from 1911 to 1965. A special daily train, known as the Lancing Belle, brought the workers from Brighton.

LAC-SSE.name: Brighton City Airport
LAC-SSE.text: Your train passes near Shoreham Airport, on the train's {side}, the oldest airport in the UK. The first flight from here was in 1910, it opened officially in 1911, and its terminal is a listed 1930s Art Deco building.

SSE-SWK.name: Shoreham Redoubt
SSE-SWK.text: Your train passes near Shoreham Fort, on the train's {side}, built at the mouth of the River Adur and finished in June 1857, at a time of political alarm. Its gun platform is shaped like a straight-sided crescent, ringed by a ditch with a loopholed wall along the middle.

FSG-SWK.name: St Michael and All Angels Church, Southwick
FSG-SWK.text: Your train passes near St Michael and All Angels Church in Southwick, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in the 12th and 13th centuries with some Anglo-Saxon work still in place. A church may have stood here as early as the 10th century.

FSG-PLD.name: Portslade Town Hall
FSG-PLD.text: Your train passes near Portslade Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built in 1928 as the Ronuk Hall, a social club for the workers of a local polish factory. It later became the meeting place of the town's council.

AGT-PLD.name: British Engineerium
AGT-PLD.text: Your train passes near the Goldstone Pumping Station in Hove, on the train's {side}, a set of High Victorian Gothic buildings begun in 1866. It pumped water for Hove and Brighton for more than a century, and later became the British Engineerium, a museum of engineering and steam power.

AGT-HOV.name: Goldstone Ground
AGT-HOV.text: Your train passes the site of the Goldstone Ground, on the train's {side}, home of Brighton & Hove Albion from 1902 to 1997. It hosted football at the 1948 Olympic Games, and David Beckham made his professional debut here in 1992.

HOV-PRP.name: Preston Manor
HOV-PRP.text: Your train passes near Preston Manor, on the train's {side}, a manor house rebuilt in 1738 around part of a 13th-century building. It has been a museum of Edwardian life since 1932, and is said to be one of the most haunted buildings in Britain.

BTN-HOV.name: St Bartholomew's Church, Brighton
BTN-HOV.text: Your train passes near St Bartholomew's Church in Brighton, on the train's {side}, opened in 1874. It has no tower or spire, but its roof rises 135 feet; one of its critics called it "a Noah's Ark in brick".

BTN-PRP.name: London Road Viaduct
BTN-PRP.text: Your train passes near the London Road Viaduct, on the train's {side}, which carries the line to Lewes across a valley in Brighton. Built in 1846, it curves sharply on 27 arches and took about ten million bricks.

HSK-PRP.name: Clayton Tunnel
HSK-PRP.text: Your train goes through Clayton Tunnel, more than a mile long and finished in 1841, the longest tunnel on the line to Brighton. Its northern entrance is turreted like a castle, with a small cottage perched on top.

BUG-HSK.name: St John the Evangelist's Church, Burgess Hill
BUG-HSK.text: Your train passes near St John the Evangelist's Church in Burgess Hill, on the train's {side}, a Gothic Revival church of local brick consecrated in 1863. It was the town's first Church of England church.

BUG-WVF.name: Burgess Hill
BUG-WVF.text: Your train passes through Burgess Hill, whose town centre is on the train's {side}. Until the 19th century much of it was St John's Common, grazing land where a Midsummer Fair was held every June 24th.

PMP-WVF.name: Plumpton Racecourse
PMP-WVF.text: Your train passes near Plumpton Racecourse, on the train's {side}, where racing began in 1884. The Queen Mother had her first winner here in 1963, and AP McCoy won his 3,000th race here in 2009.

HHE-WVF.name: Battle of Muster Green
HHE-WVF.text: Your train passes near Muster Green in Haywards Heath, on the train's {side}, where Parliamentarians beat a larger Royalist army in December 1642. It was the furthest any large Royalist force got into Sussex during the Civil Wars.

BAB-HHE.name: Ouse Valley Viaduct
BAB-HHE.text: Your train crosses the Ouse Valley Viaduct, 96 feet high and carried on 37 arches, with stone balustrades along the top. It opened to trains in July 1841, and has been called "probably the most elegant viaduct in Britain".

BAB-TBD.name: Worth Forest
BAB-TBD.text: Your train passes near Worth Forest, on the train's {side}, an ancient wood in a ghyll, a narrow valley that a stream has cut into soft sandstone. Its wet valley floor is carpeted with sphagnum moss.

CRW-TBD.name: Tree House, Crawley
CRW-TBD.text: Your train passes near Tree House on Crawley's High Street, on the train's {side}, the town's original manor house, built in the early 15th century. It is named after an ancient elm that stood outside for hundreds of years, and is now home to Crawley Museum.

CRW-IFI.name: The George Hotel, Crawley
CRW-IFI.text: Your train passes near the George in Crawley, on the train's {side}, once the most important coaching inn in Sussex, halfway between London and Brighton. Its inn sign, which reaches across the High Street, began as a gallows.

FGT-IFI.name: Ifield Water Mill
FGT-IFI.text: Your train passes near Ifield Water Mill, on the train's {side}, a weatherboarded 19th-century mill on the site of an earlier iron forge. It fell out of use in the 1930s; volunteers later restored it to working order.

FGT-LVN.name: Roffey Road Halt
FGT-LVN.text: Your train passes the site of Roffey Road Halt, opened in 1907 for steam railmotors in the hope that houses would be built nearby. They weren't, and it closed in 1937; a few concrete posts from its platforms are all that remain.

HRH-LVN.name: Horsham Museum
HRH-LVN.text: Your train passes near Horsham Museum, on the train's {side}, founded in 1893 by volunteers from the town's Free Christian Church. It has been in Causeway House, a building listed Grade II*, since 1941.

CHH-HRH.name: Chesworth House
CHH-HRH.text: Your train passes near Chesworth House, on the train's {side}, a Tudor manor house of the Dukes of Norfolk. Catherine Howard spent her childhood here before she married Henry VIII, who had stayed here himself in 1519.

BIG-CHH.name: Christ's Hospital
BIG-CHH.text: Your train passes near Christ's Hospital, on the train's {side}, a school founded in London in 1552 as a charity for poor children. Its pupils still wear a Tudor uniform of long blue coats and yellow socks, worn since 1553.

BIG-PUL.name: Old Swan Bridge, Pulborough
BIG-PUL.text: Your train passes near the Old Swan Bridge over the River Arun at Pulborough, on the train's {side}, built in 1787 in a medieval style. It replaced a line of timber bridges, and before them a ferry.

AMY-PUL.name: St Botolph's Church, Hardham
AMY-PUL.text: Your train passes near St Botolph's Church at Hardham, on the train's {side}, whose 12th-century wall paintings are the earliest nearly complete series in England. Among them is the earliest known picture of St George in the country.

AMY-ARU.name: Amberley Museum
AMY-ARU.text: Your train passes near Amberley Museum, on the train's {side}, an open-air museum of industry in an old chalk quarry. The quarry had its own railway, linked to the main line at Amberley station; the museum runs passenger trains on a narrow-gauge line today.

HRH-WNH.name: College of Richard Collyer
HRH-WNH.text: Your train passes near the College of Richard Collyer, on the train's {side}, founded in the will of Richard Collyer, a Horsham man who became a wealthy London mercer, in 1532. The Mercers' Company are still its trustees.

OLY-WNH.name: Shiremark Mill, Capel
OLY-WNH.text: Your train passes the site of Shiremark Mill, on the train's {side}, a windmill built in 1774 just inside Surrey, close to the border with Sussex. It worked by wind until 1919, and burnt down in 1972.

HLM-OLY.name: Ockley station
HLM-OLY.text: Ockley station, at one end of this stretch, opened as Ockley & Capel in 1867. Next to brickworks, it carried bricks for many years, and milk until the 1930s; it is listed Grade II.

DKG-HLM.name: Church of St Mary, Pixham
DKG-HLM.text: Your train passes near the church of St Mary at Pixham, on the train's {side}, designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens in 1903. Inside, it has a barrel-vaulted ceiling.

BXW-DKG.name: Denbies Wine Estate
BXW-DKG.text: Your train passes near Denbies Wine Estate, on the train's {side}, the largest vineyard in England, with more than a tenth of all the vines planted in the United Kingdom. It takes its name from John Denby, who owned the farmhouse here in the 16th century.

BXW-LHD.name: The Running Horse, Leatherhead
BXW-LHD.text: Your train passes near the Running Horse in Leatherhead, on the train's {side}, a pub by the River Mole dating back to 1403. It was first known as Rummings House, after Eleynor Rumminge, the subject of a poem by John Skelton, Henry VIII's poet; the poem is on a wall inside.

BKA-LHD.name: Thorndike Theatre
BKA-LHD.text: Your train passes near the Leatherhead Theatre, on the train's {side}, built inside a disused 1930s cinema and opened by Princess Margaret in 1969 as the Thorndike Theatre. It was named after the actor Dame Sybil Thorndike.

BKA-EFF.name: Bookham Commons
BKA-EFF.text: Your train passes near Bookham Commons, on the train's {side}, woods and grassland owned by the National Trust and mentioned in the Domesday Book. A group of houses on the commons is called the Isle of Wight.

EFF-HSY.name: The Forest and the Highlands
EFF-HSY.text: Your train passes near the Forest and the Highlands, on the train's {side}, a wood owned by East Horsley's parish council where almost 180 kinds of plant and more than 50 kinds of bird have been recorded, among them tawny owls and nuthatches.

CLA-HSY.name: West Horsley Place
CLA-HSY.text: Your train passes near West Horsley Place, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed house of the 15th century with 50 rooms. It is best known as the filming location of the BBC series Ghosts.

CLA-LRD.name: Abbot's Hospital
CLA-LRD.text: Your train passes near Abbot's Hospital on Guildford's High Street, on the train's {side}, founded in 1619 by George Abbot, Archbishop of Canterbury, as homes for the town's elderly. Its first residents moved in on his 60th birthday in 1622.

GLD-LRD.name: Royal Grammar School, Guildford
GLD-LRD.text: Your train passes near the Royal Grammar School in Guildford, on the train's {side}, founded in the will of Robert Beckingham, who died in 1509. Its Old Building, put up between 1557 and 1586, holds a rare chained library.

CSD-EFF.name: Cobham Training Centre
CSD-EFF.text: Your train passes near Chelsea Football Club's training ground, on the train's {side}. The first team have trained here at Stoke d'Abernon since 2005.

CSD-OXS.name: St Mary's Church, Stoke d'Abernon
CSD-OXS.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at Stoke d'Abernon, on the train's {side}, parts of which date from the 7th century. In front of the altar rail is the brass of Sir John d'Abernon, who died in 1277, one of the finest in existence.

CLG-OXS.name: Oxshott Heath and Woods
CLG-OXS.text: Your train passes near Oxshott Heath, on the train's {side}, common land of woods and heath on a sandy hill. From its top, which has a war memorial, you can see as far as Box Hill.

CLG-HYW.name: Scilly Isles, Surrey
CLG-HYW.text: Your train passes near the Scilly Isles, on the train's {side}: not the islands, but a double roundabout built in the 1930s. Drivers called its unfamiliar traffic islands the "silly islands", and the name stuck.

HYW-SUR.name: Surbiton Studios
HYW-SUR.text: Your train passes near the site of Surbiton Studios, on the train's {side}, a film studio opened in 1918 whose first film came out in January 1919. It belonged to Stoll Pictures, one of the largest British film companies of the early 1920s.

ESH-SUR.name: Seething Wells
ESH-SUR.text: Your train passes near Seething Wells, on the train's {side}, where the Lambeth Waterworks opened in 1852 to take cleaner water from the Thames above the tide. It played a part in John Snow's study of cholera in London.

ESH-HER.name: Wayneflete Tower
ESH-HER.text: Your train passes near Wayneflete Tower, on the train's {side}, the gatehouse of a palace built at Esher in 1462 by William Waynflete, Bishop of Winchester. Most of the palace was pulled down in the 17th century, but the tower survives, listed Grade I.

HER-WAL.name: Ashley Park, Surrey
HER-WAL.text: Your train passes near Ashley Park, on the train's {side}, where a grand country house stood from 1605 until the early 1920s. Its owners included the Duke of Dorset and members of the Sassoon family; its grounds are now streets of detached houses.

WAL-WYB.name: Oatlands Palace
WAL-WYB.text: Your train passes near Oatlands, on the train's {side}, where Henry VIII acquired a manor house in 1538 and rebuilt it as a palace for Anne of Cleves. Much of its foundation stone came from Chertsey Abbey; little of the palace remains.

SUR-THD.name: Giggs Hill Green
SUR-THD.text: Your train passes near Giggs Hill Green in Thames Ditton, on the train's {side}, a triangular green where the village has played cricket since 1833. Despite its name, there is no hill.

HMC-THD.name: Hampton Court Palace
HMC-THD.text: Your train passes near Hampton Court Palace, on the train's {side}. Building began in 1514 for Cardinal Wolsey, who gave it to Henry VIII in 1529; in the 1690s William III rebuilt much of it to rival the Palace of Versailles.

AHD-LHD.name: Ashtead Common
AHD-LHD.text: Your train passes near Ashtead Common, on the train's {side}, a wood with more than 2,300 pollarded oaks, many of them 300 to 400 years old. It belongs to the City of London, and much of it is a National Nature Reserve.

AHD-EPS.name: Epsom
AHD-EPS.text: Your train passes through Epsom, whose town centre is on the train's {side}. In the late 17th century a spring on Epsom Common was thought to heal, and its water was rich in what became known as Epsom salts.

EPS-EWW.name: Bugby Chapel
EPS-EWW.text: Your train passes near Bugby Chapel in Epsom, on the train's {side}, built in 1779 by a Calvinist preacher, William Bugby. It was later a Baptist chapel and, from 1954, a synagogue; since 1994 it has been an office.

EPS-EWE.name: Laine Theatre Arts
EPS-EWE.text: Your train passes Laine Theatre Arts in Epsom, on the train's {side}, a college for dance and musical theatre founded in 1974 by the dancer Betty Laine. Victoria Beckham trained there.

CHE-EWE.name: Nonsuch Palace
CHE-EWE.text: Your train passes near the site of Nonsuch Palace, on the train's {side}, begun by Henry VIII in 1538 to rival the French king's Château de Chambord. It was pulled down in 1682 and 1683 by Barbara, Countess of Castlemaine, who sold the materials to pay her gambling debts.

EWW-SNL.name: Fitznells Manor
EWW-SNL.text: Your train passes near Fitznells Manor in Ewell, on the train's {side}, the last surviving manor house in the borough of Epsom and Ewell. Its oldest part is a wing of a timber-framed hall house probably built in the early 16th century.

SNL-WCP.name: Stoneleigh station
SNL-WCP.text: Stoneleigh station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1932. It is in London fare zone 5, and is the only National Rail station in that zone that isn't in a London borough.

GTW-TBD.name: The Beehive, Gatwick Airport
GTW-TBD.text: Your train passes near the Beehive, on the train's {side}, Gatwick's first terminal: a round building opened in 1936, when passengers came by fast train from London Victoria to fly to Paris. It is now offices.

CBR-PMP.name: East Chiltington
CBR-PMP.text: Your train passes near East Chiltington, on the train's {side}, a village whose church is 13th century in origin. A Roman road, the Sussex Greensand Way, runs through the middle of its parish.

CBR-LWS.name: Lewes Castle
CBR-LWS.text: Your train passes near Lewes Castle, on the train's {side}, built by William de Warenne after the Norman Conquest. Unusually it has two mottes, or mounds; the only other castle in England like it is Lincoln Castle.

FMR-LWS.name: The Greenwich meridian
FMR-LWS.text: Your train crosses the Greenwich meridian on the edge of Lewes, a town that sits on the line of zero longitude. The Greenwich Meridian Trail, a long walk from Peacehaven to East Yorkshire, passes through the middle of the town.

FMR-MCB.name: Falmer Stadium
FMR-MCB.text: Your train passes near Falmer Stadium, known as the Amex, on the train's {side}: home of Brighton & Hove Albion since 2011, with room for 32,500. It has also held matches in the 2015 Rugby World Cup and the Women's Euro 2022.

LRB-MCB.name: Moulsecoomb Place
LRB-MCB.text: Your train passes near Moulsecoomb Place, on the train's {side}, a farmhouse remodelled as a Neoclassical mansion in 1790. The council bought it between the wars, when Moulsecoomb became a large council estate, and it later became part of the University of Brighton.

BTN-LRB.name: Brighton Toy and Model Museum
BTN-LRB.text: Your train passes near the Brighton Toy and Model Museum, on the train's {side}, which fills four Victorian arches under the forecourt of Brighton station. Founded in 1991, it holds more than 10,000 toys and models.

LWS-SEE.name: Lewes Priory
LWS-SEE.text: Your train passes near the ruins of Lewes Priory, on the train's {side}, the first Cluniac priory in England. In 1264, after losing the Battle of Lewes, Henry III retreated there and was forced to accept a council that marked the start of parliamentary government in England.

GLY-LWS.name: Mount Caburn
GLY-LWS.text: Your train passes near Mount Caburn, on the train's {side}, a 150-metre hill with an Iron Age hill fort on top. It has been dug so often, with 170 trenches, that it may have had more excavations than any other site in Britain.

BRK-GLY.name: Glynde Place
BRK-GLY.text: Your train passes near Glynde Place, on the train's {side}, an Elizabethan manor house built in 1569 and still the family home of the Viscounts Hampden. Since 2013 its grounds have held the Love Supreme Jazz Festival every summer.

BRK-PLG.name: Ovenden's Mill, Polegate
BRK-PLG.text: Your train passes near Ovenden's Mill in Polegate, on the train's {side}, a four-storey brick tower mill built in 1817. It worked by wind until 1943, and then by engine until 1965.

HMD-PLG.name: Hampden Park
HMD-PLG.text: Your train passes through Hampden Park, a suburb of Eastbourne on the train's {side}. Trains on the East Coastway Line often pass through its station twice, and its level crossing is thought to be one of the busiest in Europe.

HMD-PEV.name: Stone Cross Windmill
HMD-PEV.text: Your train passes near Stone Cross Windmill, on the train's {side}, built in 1876 and worked by wind until 1937. It was a lookout post in the Second World War, and after a long restoration it was making wholemeal flour again in 2000.

EBN-HMD.name: Eastbourne
EBN-HMD.text: Your train passes through Eastbourne, whose town centre is on the train's {side}. The seaside resort lies just east of Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in Great Britain.

PEB-PEV.name: Pevensey Castle
PEB-PEV.text: Your train passes near Pevensey Castle, on the train's {side}, a Roman fort called Anderitum built around 290 AD. The Normans reoccupied it in 1066 and built a castle inside its walls; it was besieged several times but never taken by storm.

NSB-PEB.name: St Nicolas' Church, Pevensey
NSB-PEB.text: Your train passes near St Nicolas' Church in Pevensey, on the train's {side}, built between 1205 and 1216 and named after the patron saint of seafarers. Its size reflects Pevensey's importance as a seaport then; the sea is now about half a mile away.

COB-NSB.name: Normans Bay
COB-NSB.text: Your train passes Normans Bay, a coastal hamlet on the train's {side}, called Pevensey Sluice until the railway halt opened in 1905. In 2005 divers found cannons offshore, perhaps from a Dutch warship sunk in the Battle of Beachy Head in 1690.

CLL-COB.name: Gillham Wood
CLL-COB.text: Your train passes Gillham Wood, on the train's {side}, a Sussex Wildlife Trust reserve of oak with hazel, birch and holly. An old bomb crater in it is now a pond, and 74 kinds of bird have been recorded there.

BEX-CLL.name: De La Warr Pavilion
BEX-CLL.text: Your train passes near the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill, on the train's {side}, built in 1935 and described by Historic England as the UK's first public building in the Modernist style. Since 2005 it has been an arts centre.

BEX-WLD.name: SM UB-131
BEX-WLD.text: Your train passes near Bulverhythe, on the train's {side}, where a German submarine from the First World War, UB-131, was wrecked in January 1921 while being towed from Harwich to Falmouth for explosive trials. The wreck was sold for £655 and broken up where it lay.

CWU-WLD.name: St Leonards West Marina station
CWU-WLD.text: Your train passes near the site of St Leonards West Marina station, on the train's {side}, opened in 1846 and caught up in a feud between two rival railway companies over the way into Hastings. It closed in 1967.

BAT-CWU.name: Senlac Hill
BAT-CWU.text: Your train passes near Senlac Hill, on the train's {side}, where Harold is generally thought to have placed his army for the Battle of Hastings on October 14th 1066. Battle Abbey was later built on top of it.

BAT-RBR.name: Glottenham Castle
BAT-RBR.text: Your train passes near the site of Glottenham Castle, on the train's {side}, built in the late 13th century with stone walls, two square towers and a gatehouse. It belonged to the de Etchingham family and was abandoned by the 17th century.

ETC-RBR.name: Robertsbridge
ETC-RBR.text: Your train passes Robertsbridge, on the train's {side}, a village thought to date from 1176, when a Cistercian abbey was founded there. A 14th-century manuscript found here, the Robertsbridge Codex, holds the earliest surviving music written for keyboard.

ETC-SOG.name: Etchingham church
ETC-SOG.text: Your train passes near Etchingham's 14th-century church, on the train's {side}, whose spire carries what is probably England's oldest brass weather vane. The village's medieval manor house stood where the railway now runs.

SOG-WAD.name: Wadhurst Castle
SOG-WAD.text: Your train passes near Wadhurst Castle, on the train's {side}, a castle-style mansion first built between 1818 and 1820 and remodelled for Benjamin Harding, who bought it in 1838. It is now a wedding venue.

FRT-WAD.name: Frant station
FRT-WAD.text: Frant station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1851. It stands in the hamlet of Bells Yew Green, about two kilometres from the village of Frant itself.

FRT-TBW.name: The Pantiles
FRT-TBW.text: Your train passes near the Pantiles in Tunbridge Wells, on the train's {side}, a Georgian colonnade leading from the iron-rich spring, found in 1606, that gave the town its name. In summer, costumed 'dippers' serve the water to visitors.

HIB-TBW.name: Trinity Theatre
HIB-TBW.text: Your train passes near Trinity Theatre in Tunbridge Wells, on the train's {side}, which was Holy Trinity Church from 1829 to 1972. Decimus Burton designed it, in sandstone from Calverley Quarry; it is now a theatre and arts centre.

HIB-TON.name: Tonbridge Castle
HIB-TON.text: Your train passes near Tonbridge Castle, on the train's {side}, first built after the Norman Conquest to guard the crossing of the River Medway. Its twin-towered gatehouse took 30 years to build and was finished in 1260.

LIH-TON.name: Haysden Country Park
LIH-TON.text: Your train passes Haysden Country Park, on the train's {side}, opened in 1988 on the edge of Tonbridge. It has two lakes, Barden Lake and Haysden Water, and the River Medway runs through it.

LIH-PHR.name: Penshurst Place
LIH-PHR.text: Your train passes the park of Penshurst Place, on the train's {side}. The house was built in 1341 for Sir John de Pulteney, four times Lord Mayor of London, and the poet Sir Philip Sidney was born there in 1554.

EBR-PHR.name: Jaques of London
EBR-PHR.text: Your train passes near Jaques of London, on the train's {side}, a games maker dating from 1795 that moved to Edenbridge in 2000. In 1849 it brought out the Staunton chess set, which became the international standard.

EBR-GDN.name: Crowhurst Yew
EBR-GDN.text: Your train passes near the Crowhurst Yew, on the train's {side}, in the churchyard at Crowhurst. It is thought to be about 4,000 years old; when a hollow was cut into it in 1820, a cannonball was found embedded in its side.

GDN-NUF.name: Brewing Industry Research Foundation
GDN-NUF.text: Your train passes near Lyttel Hall at Nutfield, on the train's {side}, bought in 1948 for the Brewing Industry Research Foundation. Its squash court became a pilot brewery, and brewing research went on there until 2024.

NUF-RDH.name: Redhill Tunnel
NUF-RDH.text: Coming into Redhill, your train passes over the covered way at the end of Redhill Tunnel. The tunnel, opened in 1899, takes the Quarry Line of the Brighton Main Line under the east of the town, so that its trains avoid Redhill station.

MHM-RDH.name: Gatton
MHM-RDH.text: Your train passes near Gatton, on the train's {side}, now just a few houses and two farms. It once sent two members to Parliament: by 1831 it had only seven voters, one of the most notorious rotten boroughs, until the Reform Act of 1832 abolished it.

CDS-MHM.name: Merstham Tunnel
CDS-MHM.text: Your train runs through Merstham Tunnel under the North Downs, opened in 1841 for the first railway from London to Brighton. Nearly 60 years later the Quarry Tunnel was built beside it, which most fast trains now use.

HLB-TON.name: Tonbridge Priory
HLB-TON.text: Your train passes the site of Tonbridge Priory, on the train's {side}, founded in 1124. Its last remains were demolished in 1842 when the South Eastern Railway came through, and Tonbridge's first station was built on the site.

HLB-SEV.name: Knole
HLB-SEV.text: Your train passes near Knole Park, on the train's {side}, a deer park of 1,000 acres. Its house, Knole, was once an archbishop's palace and is one of the five largest houses in England; the National Trust owns it.

DNG-SEV.name: Vine Cricket Ground
DNG-SEV.text: Your train passes near the Vine Cricket Ground in Sevenoaks, on the train's {side}, one of the oldest cricket grounds in England, first known to be used in 1734. The Duke of Dorset gave it to the town in 1773, for a rent of one peppercorn a year.

DNG-KCK.name: Polhill Anglo-Saxon cemetery
DNG-KCK.text: Your train passes near the site of the Polhill Anglo-Saxon cemetery, on the train's {side}, used in the seventh and eighth centuries. It held between 180 and 200 graves; its east end was dug in 1984, ahead of work on the M25.

BBL-SEV.name: Sevenoaks Gravel Pits
BBL-SEV.text: Your train passes near the Sevenoaks Wildlife Reserve, on the train's {side}, made from old gravel pits by the Harrison family. It was the first gravel pit in the United Kingdom turned into a nature reserve, and has five lakes filled from the River Darent.

BBL-OTF.name: Otford Roman villa
BBL-OTF.text: Your train passes near the site of a Roman villa at Otford, on the train's {side}, abandoned in the fourth century. Its remains were found and dug in the 1930s, and again in 2015.

OTF-SEH.name: Otford Palace
OTF-SEH.text: Your train passes near the ruins of Otford Palace, on the train's {side}, rebuilt by Archbishop Warham from 1514. Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon stayed there in 1520 on their way to the Field of the Cloth of Gold, and in 1537 Henry made Archbishop Cranmer hand it over to the Crown.

EYN-SEH.name: Lullingstone Roman Villa
EYN-SEH.text: Your train passes near Lullingstone Roman Villa, on the train's {side}, first built around AD 82. In the fourth century one of its rooms became a Christian chapel or house church, the earliest known in the British Isles.

EYN-SAY.name: Eynsford Castle
EYN-SAY.text: Your train passes near Eynsford Castle, on the train's {side}, a ruin now looked after by English Heritage. William de Eynsford built it, probably between 1085 and 1087, to protect the lands of the Archbishop of Canterbury.

FNR-SAY.name: St John's Jerusalem
FNR-SAY.text: Your train passes near St John's Jerusalem, on the train's {side}, set up in 1199 by the Knights Hospitaller. Its 13th-century chapel and a garden moated by the River Darent belong to the National Trust and are open to the public.

FNR-LGF.name: South Darenth viaduct
FNR-LGF.text: Your train crosses the viaduct at South Darenth, built in 1859 and 1860 to a design by Joseph Cubitt. It has ten arches, each about 20 metres high, and one of them spans the River Darent.

AFK-FNR.name: White Horse Stone
AFK-FNR.text: Your train passes near the White Horse Stone, on the train's {side}, a sarsen stone on Blue Bell Hill. Excavators found a Neolithic longhouse just south of it, 18 metres long, in use some time between about 4100 and 3500 BC.

AFK-EBD.name: Medway Viaduct
AFK-EBD.text: Your train crosses the River Medway on the viaduct of the high-speed line to the Channel Tunnel, finished in 2002 beside the two bridges of the M2. In 2003 a specially formed Eurostar crossed it at 208 mph, a new speed record for Britain's railways.

EBD-GRV.name: Baker's Hole
EBD-GRV.text: Your train passes near Baker's Hole, on the train's {side}, a filled-in quarry by Ebbsfleet. Quarrymen there found many Stone Age flint tools from 1909, and it has been called the best known site in Britain from its part of the Old Stone Age.

GRV-NFL.name: St George's Church, Gravesend
GRV-NFL.text: Your train passes near St George's Church in Gravesend, on the train's {side}, where Pocahontas was buried in 1617. She died in Gravesend aged 20 or 21, on her way home to America; a bronze statue of her stands by the church.

NFL-SWM.name: Stonebridge Road
NFL-SWM.text: Your train passes near Stonebridge Road, on the train's {side}, the football ground built in 1905 for Northfleet United. It is the home of Ebbsfleet United, and holds 4,769 people.

GNH-SWM.name: Swanscombe Skull Site
GNH-SWM.text: Your train passes near the Swanscombe Skull Site, on the train's {side}, an old gravel pit. In 1935 and 1936 an amateur found pieces of a human skull there, about 400,000 years old, probably from an early Neanderthal or Homo heidelbergensis.

GNH-SCG.name: Ingress Abbey
GNH-SCG.text: Your train passes near Ingress Abbey, on the train's {side}, a mansion built by the Thames in 1833 for the solicitor James Harmer. Harmer served as a model for Jaggers, the lawyer in Dickens's Great Expectations.

DFD-SCG.name: Holy Trinity Church, Dartford
DFD-SCG.text: Your train passes near Holy Trinity Church in Dartford, on the train's {side}, begun in about 1080 by Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester. A painting of St George slaying the dragon, from about 1485, can still be seen on one of its walls.

CRY-DFD.name: Dartford Priory
CRY-DFD.text: Your train passes near what is left of Dartford Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of Dominican nuns founded by Edward III. Henry VIII took it for himself and turned it into a royal manor house; its gatehouse survives in a farmhouse.

GRV-HGM.name: Guru Nanak Darbar Gurdwara
GRV-HGM.text: Your train passes the Guru Nanak Darbar Gurdwara in Gravesend, on the train's {side}, one of the largest Sikh gurdwaras outside India. It opened in 2010, at a cost of £12 million.

HGM-SOO.name: Higham and Strood tunnel
HGM-SOO.text: Your train runs through the Higham and Strood tunnel, 3.5 km long, dug by hand for the Thames and Medway Canal. From 1845 trains shared it with the barges, on a single track resting partly on the towpath. In 1846 the railway bought the tunnel, filled in the canal and laid two tracks.

CUX-SOO.name: Temple Manor
CUX-SOO.text: Your train passes Temple Manor in Strood, on the train's {side}, built in the early 13th century for the Knights Templar. When the Templars were suppressed in 1312 it passed to the Knights Hospitaller; English Heritage now opens it to visitors.

CUX-HAI.name: Ranscombe Farm
CUX-HAI.text: Your train passes near Ranscombe Farm, on the train's {side}, a working farm and Plantlife nature reserve. It is known for rare plants of farmland and chalk grassland, such as hairy mallow, ground pine and the lady orchid.

HAI-SDA.name: Holborough Marshes
HAI-SDA.text: Your train passes Holborough Marshes, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of 35 hectares on the edge of Snodland, run by Kent Wildlife Trust. It has reedbeds and wet grassland, with water voles, reed buntings and sedge warblers.

NHE-SDA.name: All Saints Church, Snodland
NHE-SDA.text: Your train passes near All Saints Church in Snodland, on the train's {side}, which stands where the Pilgrims' Way crosses the River Medway. It is mentioned in the Domesday Book of 1086, and the church standing today was begun in the 12th century.

AYL-NHE.name: Aylesford Priory
AYL-NHE.text: Your train passes near Aylesford Priory, The Friars, on the train's {side}, founded in 1242 by Carmelite friars who came from Mount Carmel in the Holy Land. The Carmelites came back in 1949, and it is a place of pilgrimage once more.

AYL-MDB.name: Allington Castle
AYL-MDB.text: Your train passes near Allington Castle, on the train's {side}, home of Sir Thomas Wyatt the Younger until the Crown seized it in 1554, after his rebellion against Queen Mary. Largely a ruin by the early 1900s, it was saved and restored by Sir Martin Conway and his wife.

MDB-MDW.name: Archbishop's Palace, Maidstone
MDB-MDW.text: Your train passes near the Archbishop's Palace in Maidstone, on the train's {side}, by the River Medway. It was a resting place for archbishops travelling between London and Canterbury, and work on the present building began in 1348.

EFL-MDW.name: East Farleigh Bridge
EFL-MDW.text: Your train passes East Farleigh Bridge, on the train's {side}, probably built in the 14th century and still carrying traffic, one way at a time, over the Medway. It has been described as probably the finest medieval bridge in the south of England.

EFL-WTR.name: Teston Bridge
EFL-WTR.text: Your train passes Teston Bridge, on the train's {side}, a narrow bridge over the Medway built in the 14th or 15th century. The line crosses its road on the level, where Teston Crossing Halt stood from 1909 to 1959.

WTR-YAL.name: Nettlestead Place
WTR-YAL.text: Your train passes Nettlestead Place, on the train's {side}, a ragstone house begun around 1250. It was used as an oast house for two centuries before it was restored as a home in the 1920s.

BEG-YAL.name: The Hop Farm
BEG-YAL.text: Your train passes near the Hop Farm at Beltring, on the train's {side}, where hops have been grown since at least the 16th century. It has the largest collection of oast houses in the world, and once grew hops for Whitbread.

BEG-PDW.name: The John Brunt V.C.
BEG-PDW.text: Your train passes the John Brunt V.C. pub in Paddock Wood, on the train's {side}. Once the Kent Arms, it was renamed in 1947 after John Brunt, who spent his teenage years in the town and won the Victoria Cross in the Second World War.

PDW-TON.name: Somerhill House
PDW-TON.text: Your train passes near Somerhill House, on the train's {side}, a Jacobean mansion built from 1611 to 1613 for the Earl of Clanricarde. Turner painted it in 1811, and it is now a school.

MRN-PDW.name: St Michael and All Angels Church, Marden
MRN-PDW.text: Your train passes near St Michael and All Angels Church, Marden, on the train's {side}, built at the end of the 12th century. The church is the picture on the village sign.

MRN-SPU.name: Marden Meadows
MRN-SPU.text: Your train passes Marden Meadows, on the train's {side}, three fields of unimproved grassland that are a Site of Special Scientific Interest. They are mown for hay once a year, and green-winged orchids grow there.

HCN-SPU.name: St Peter and St Paul's Church, Headcorn
HCN-SPU.text: Your train passes near Headcorn's parish church, on the train's {side}. By its south door are the remains of the Headcorn Oak, said to be up to 1,200 years old, though one expert reckoned it nearer 500.

HCN-PLC.name: Headcorn Aerodrome
HCN-PLC.text: Your train passes near Headcorn Aerodrome, on the train's {side}, a grass airfield that opened in 1943 as RAF Lashenden, a name chosen to confuse the enemy. Today it is home to Kent's only skydiving club.

AFK-PLC.name: Godinton Park
AFK-PLC.text: Your train runs beside Godinton Park, on the train's {side}. Its Jacobean house was home to the Toke family for about 455 years, and its garden has one of the longest yew hedges in England.

AFK-CHG.name: Archbishop's Palace, Charing
AFK-CHG.text: Your train passes near the Archbishop's Palace at Charing, on the train's {side}, one of the earliest properties of the archbishops of Canterbury. In 1520 Henry VIII stayed here with an entourage of more than 5,000 on his way to the Field of the Cloth of Gold.

CHG-LEN.name: St Mary's Church, Lenham
CHG-LEN.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Lenham, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in the 14th century after a fire destroyed the one before. It and the nearby tithe barn are both Grade I listed.

HRM-LEN.name: Bell Farm House
HRM-LEN.text: Your train passes near Bell Farm House in Harrietsham, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed farmhouse built around 1500. Its hall wall is still blackened by smoke from the days before it had a chimney.

HBN-HRM.name: Leeds Castle
HBN-HRM.text: Your train passes within a kilometre of the parkland of Leeds Castle, on the train's {side}. The castle stands on islands in a lake made by the River Len; Henry VIII used it as a home for his first wife, Catherine of Aragon.

BSD-HBN.name: Holy Cross Church, Bearsted
BSD-HBN.text: Your train passes near Holy Cross Church, Bearsted, on the train's {side}, begun in the 13th century. Three stone beasts sit on the corners of its tower, replacing worn originals that may have shown wolves from a family coat of arms.

BSD-MDE.name: Mote Park
BSD-MDE.text: Your train passes near Mote Park, on the train's {side}, a public park of about 450 acres in Maidstone. Its name comes from an Old English word for a place of assembly, and it has a boating lake and a miniature railway.

BMG-MDE.name: Maidstone Museum
BMG-MDE.text: Your train passes near Maidstone Museum, on the train's {side}, built round Chillington Manor, an Elizabethan house finished in 1577. It opened in 1858 with the collections of a local doctor, and has one of the most important Japanese collections outside London.

BMG-EML.name: East Malling Research Station
BMG-EML.text: Your train passes near the fruit research station at East Malling, on the train's {side}, set up in 1913. Its research, above all on rootstocks for fruit trees, earned it a worldwide reputation.

EML-WMA.name: St James the Great's Church, East Malling
EML-WMA.text: Your train passes near St James the Great's Church, East Malling, on the train's {side}, with a nave of the 14th century. Sir Thomas Twisden lies here, a judge at the trials of the regicides of Charles I.

BRG-WMA.name: Malling Abbey
BRG-WMA.text: Your train passes near Malling Abbey in West Malling, on the train's {side}, founded for Benedictine nuns around 1090 by Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester. It was dissolved in 1538, became a monastery again in the late 19th century, and is now home to Anglican Benedictine nuns.

BRG-KMS.name: Oldbury Hill
BRG-KMS.text: Your train passes near the Iron Age hillfort on Oldbury Hill, on the train's {side}, thought to have been built around 100 BC. At 123 acres it was the largest of a line of forts across Kent and Surrey, and flint tools from the Palaeolithic have been found there too.

KMS-OTF.name: Greatness Brickworks
KMS-OTF.text: Your train passes near Greatness Brickworks, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest in Sevenoaks for its Cretaceous rocks, which are rich in fossils, above all ammonites. It is private land.

AFK-HMT.name: Newtown, Ashford
AFK-HMT.text: Your train passes Newtown, on the train's {side}, built by the South Eastern Railway from 1847 for the workers at its Ashford works. It was first called Alfred Town, and was laid out round a green.

APD-HMT.name: Royal Military Canal
APD-HMT.text: Your train crosses the Royal Military Canal, dug from 1804 along the edge of Romney Marsh as a barrier against Napoleon's planned invasion. Early in the Second World War it was fortified again, and many of its pillboxes survive.

APD-RYE.name: The Landgate, Rye
APD-RYE.text: Your train passes near the Landgate at Rye, on the train's {side}, the only one left of the town's four fortified gateways, dating from 1329. In 2015 some 25 tonnes of pigeon droppings had to be cleared from its arch.

RYE-WSE.name: Ypres Tower
RYE-WSE.text: Your train passes near Ypres Tower in Rye, on the train's {side}, built in the 13th or 14th century to defend the town and once called Baddings Tower. It was later a prison, and is now part of Rye Castle Museum.

DLH-WSE.name: Winchelsea
DLH-WSE.text: Your train passes near Winchelsea, on the train's {side}, a town planned on a grid on higher ground after storms ravaged the old town on the shingle. Edward I granted it a charter in 1281.

DLH-TOK.name: Doleham station
DLH-TOK.text: Doleham station, at one end of this stretch, is a single-platform halt that opened as Guestling Halt in 1907. It serves only a handful of houses, and before the pandemic about eight people a day used it.

ORE-TOK.name: Speckled Wood
ORE-TOK.text: Your train passes near Speckled Wood, on the train's {side}, a steep-sided, wet woodland park in Ore. It is thought to take its name from the speckled wood butterflies that thrive there.

HGS-ORE.name: Hastings Castle
HGS-ORE.text: Your train passes near Hastings Castle, on the train's {side}, begun in 1066 on William of Normandy's orders, before the Battle of Hastings. It stands on the West Hill cliffs, and large parts of it have fallen into the sea.

HGS-SLQ.name: Hastings Museum and Art Gallery
HGS-SLQ.text: Your train passes near Hastings Museum and Art Gallery, on the train's {side}, founded in 1892. Its Durbar Hall was part of an Indian palace built for the Indian and Colonial Exhibition of 1886.

SLQ-WLD.name: Marine Court
SLQ-WLD.text: Your train passes near Marine Court on the seafront at St Leonards, on the train's {side}, a block of flats built from 1936 to 1938 to look like the liner Queen Mary. Its curved eastern end steps back as it rises, like the forecastle of a ship.

AFK-WYE.name: Wye College
AFK-WYE.text: Your train passes near Wye College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1447 by Cardinal John Kempe as a chantry college that taught local children. It later became an agricultural college of the University of London, and closed in 2009.

AFK-WHA.name: Westenhanger Castle
AFK-WHA.text: Your train passes Westenhanger Castle, on the train's {side}, a fortified manor house of the 14th century. In 1588 Elizabeth I used it as the headquarters for Kent's 14,000 troops against the Spanish Armada.

SDG-WHA.name: Folkestone Racecourse
SDG-WHA.text: Your train passes near Folkestone Racecourse at Westenhanger, on the train's {side}, where racing began in 1898. It closed in 2012, and its grandstand can be seen from the station.

FKW-SDG.name: Saltwood Castle
FKW-SDG.text: Your train passes near Saltwood Castle, on the train's {side}, which belonged to the archbishops of Canterbury until 1540. In 1953 the art historian Kenneth Clark bought it, and his son, the diarist Alan Clark, lived there later.

FKC-FKW.name: Cheriton Road
FKC-FKW.text: Your train passes near the Cheriton Road sports grounds in Folkestone, on the train's {side}, home of Folkestone Invicta. Cricket has been played there since 1901, and Kent County Cricket Club has used the ground.

DVP-FKC.name: Samphire Hoe
DVP-FKC.text: Your train passes Samphire Hoe, on the train's {side}, a country park at the foot of the White Cliffs made from 4.9 million cubic metres of chalk dug out for the Channel Tunnel. It opened in 1997 and is named after rock samphire, which Shakespeare mentions in King Lear.

DVP-KSN.name: Dover Priory
DVP-KSN.text: Your train passes the remains of Dover Priory, on the train's {side}; the railway was built across the western part of its site. Dover College uses its old buildings, and the 12th-century Strangers' Refectory is still in use.

KSN-SPH.name: Lydden and Temple Ewell Downs
KSN-SPH.text: Your train passes Lydden and Temple Ewell Downs, on the train's {side}, some of the richest chalk downland in Kent, with adonis blues and silver-spotted skippers. In June 2025 the Dover twist moth was found here, not seen in England since 1952.

SPH-SWO.name: Shepherdswell (East Kent Railway)
SPH-SWO.text: Your train passes the East Kent Railway's station at Shepherdswell, on the train's {side}. It opened in 1916 as the end of the East Kent Light Railway, closed to passengers in 1948, and reopened as a heritage line in 1993.

AYH-SWO.name: Snowdown
AYH-SWO.text: Your train passes near Snowdown, on the train's {side}, a hamlet that was home to one of the four chief collieries of the Kent coalfield. The colliery closed in 1987.

ADM-AYH.name: Aylesham
ADM-AYH.text: Your train passes near Aylesham, on the train's {side}, a village begun in 1926 for miners at the newly sunk Snowdown Colliery. Its planner, Sir Patrick Abercrombie, meant it to grow into a town of up to 30,000 people.

ADM-BKS.name: Bekesbourne Aerodrome
ADM-BKS.text: Your train passes the site of Bekesbourne Aerodrome, on the train's {side}, which had the railway along its northern edge. It began in 1916 as a landing ground for the Royal Flying Corps, and from December 1918 its squadron was commanded by Arthur Harris, later Marshal of the Royal Air Force.

BKS-CBE.name: St Martin's Church, Canterbury
BKS-CBE.text: Your train passes near St Martin's Church, on the train's {side}, the oldest church building in England still in use as a church. It was Queen Bertha of Kent's private chapel before Augustine arrived from Rome in 597, and is part of Canterbury's World Heritage Site.

CBE-SEG.name: Canterbury Castle
CBE-SEG.text: Your train passes Canterbury Castle, on the train's {side}, one of the three royal castles of Kent built soon after the Battle of Hastings. Its great stone keep went up in the reign of Henry I; by the 19th century a gas company was using it for storage.

FAV-SEG.name: St Catherine's Church, Preston-next-Faversham
FAV-SEG.text: Your train passes St Catherine's Church, Preston-next-Faversham, on the train's {side}. It dates from the Norman period, and John Betjeman described it as “high and distinguished among the railways and breweries”.

FAV-TEY.name: Maison Dieu, Ospringe
FAV-TEY.text: Your train passes the Maison Dieu at Ospringe, on the train's {side}, beside Watling Street. Henry III commissioned it in 1234 as a hospital and a place for pilgrims and the poor to stay, with a chamber kept for the king to rest in when he passed this way.

SIT-TEY.name: Church of All Saints, Murston
SIT-TEY.text: Your train passes near All Saints Church, Murston, on the train's {side}, designed by William Burges and built in 1873 and 1874. Fumes from the brickworks and gasworks round the old church made it hard to breathe during services, so the rector paid £500 of his own money towards a new one away from them.

NGT-SIT.name: Watling Temple
NGT-SIT.text: Your train passes near Watling Temple in Newington, on the train's {side}: the remains of a temple in a Roman town found during a dig in 2019, along with pottery kilns and a Roman road. A reconstruction of its foundations, the same size and facing the same way, was unveiled near the spot in 2021.

NGT-RAI.name: Newington
NGT-RAI.text: Your train passes Newington, on the train's {side}. Its parish church was built between 1163 and 1177 by Richard de Lucy, and a stone in the church car park, the Devil's Stone, is said to bear the Devil's footprint. The village also holds the national collection of witch hazel.

GLM-RAI.name: Priestfield Stadium
GLM-RAI.text: Your train passes near Priestfield Stadium, on the train's {side}, home of Gillingham Football Club since the club began as New Brompton in 1893. Brighton & Hove Albion also played their home games here for two seasons in the 1990s.

CTM-GLM.name: Chatham Naval Memorial
CTM-GLM.text: Your train passes near the Chatham Naval Memorial, on the train's {side}, an obelisk on the Great Lines unveiled in 1924. It names sailors and marines of the Royal Navy lost in the First World War who have no known grave, and of the three such memorials (the others are at Portsmouth and Plymouth) it's the only one on a hill.

CTM-RTR.name: Fort Pitt
CTM-RTR.text: Your train passes Fort Pitt, on the train's {side}, a fort built between 1805 and 1819 on the high ground between Chatham and Rochester. With the Napoleonic Wars over, it became a military hospital, from 1824 to 1857 the only General Military Hospital in England. Its surviving buildings now house a girls' grammar school.

RTR-SOR.name: Rochester Castle
RTR-SOR.text: Your train passes Rochester Castle, on the train's {side}, on the bank of the Medway. Its 12th-century keep, built by William de Corbeil, Archbishop of Canterbury, is one of the best preserved of its time in England or France.

MEP-SOR.name: St Mildred's Church, Nurstead
MEP-SOR.text: Your train passes near St Mildred's, the small 14th-century church of Nurstead, on the train's {side}, its walls built of oblong flints. A quarter of a mile north of it is Nurstead Court, called one of the most famous small medieval houses in the country.

LGF-MEP.name: Longfield
LGF-MEP.text: Your train passes Longfield, on the train's {side}, recorded as Langanfelda in Saxon charters. In the mid-1940s the planner Patrick Abercrombie proposed building a new town here as part of the Greater London Plan, but other places around London were chosen instead.

RTR-SOO.name: River Medway (Rochester Bridge)
RTR-SOO.text: Your train crosses the River Medway on the railway bridge, one of the four bridges that together make up Rochester Bridge. The Romans built the first bridge here to carry Watling Street, and for centuries it was the lowest fixed crossing of the river.

KML-NGT.name: Bobbing
KML-NGT.text: Your train passes Bobbing, on the train's {side}. In 1673 the local squire made Titus Oates, later the inventor of the Popish Plot, vicar here, but his drunkenness and blasphemy so horrified the parishioners that they put him out before the end of the year.

KML-SIT.name: Kemsley
KML-SIT.text: Your train passes Kemsley, on the train's {side}, a garden village built in 1924 by Edward Lloyd for the workers at his new Kemsley Paper Mill. The narrow-gauge railway that served the mill survives as the Sittingbourne and Kemsley Light Railway.

KML-SWL.name: Ridham Dock
KML-SWL.text: Your train passes near Ridham Dock on the Swale, on the train's {side}, planned to give the Sittingbourne paper mills deeper water than the silted Milton Creek. Work began in 1913; during the First World War it was used for loading ammunition, and it was finished in 1919.

QBR-SWL.name: Kingsferry Bridge
QBR-SWL.text: Your train crosses the Swale, between the Isle of Sheppey and the mainland, on the Kingsferry Bridge, which carries road and railway together. Its middle span lifts straight up to let ships through; it replaced a bascule bridge of 1860, whose span tipped up instead.

QBR-SSS.name: Queenborough Castle
QBR-SSS.text: Your train passes the site of Queenborough Castle, on the train's {side}, built for Edward III from 1361 and named, like the town, after his wife Queen Philippa. It was the first concentric castle built in England; it was pulled down soon after 1650, and only low earthworks remain in what is now a park.

FAV-WHI.name: St Bartholomew's Church, Goodnestone
FAV-WHI.text: Your train passes near St Bartholomew's Church, Goodnestone, on the train's {side}, a small Norman church of the 12th century. Its porch had to be rebuilt in 1837 after an earth tremor damaged it; it's now cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust.

CSW-WHI.name: All Saints Church, Whitstable
CSW-WHI.text: Your train passes near All Saints Church, Whitstable, on the train's {side}, where there has been a church for at least 800 years. Its oldest brass remembers Thomas Brede, who died in 1444, and a priest's tomb slab still shows the outline of a chalice.

CSW-HNB.name: Swalecliffe
CSW-HNB.text: Your train passes Swalecliffe, on the train's {side}, recorded in the Domesday Book. In 1581 a farm here called Bodkin's was given to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and most of its income paid for four scholars.

BCH-HNB.name: Church of St Mary the Virgin, Reculver
BCH-HNB.text: Your train passes near the Church of St Mary the Virgin at Hillborough, on the train's {side}, built between 1876 and 1878. It includes materials from the church founded in 669 inside the Roman fort at Reculver, which was mostly pulled down in 1809.

BCH-WGA.name: Carlton Cinema, Westgate-on-Sea
BCH-WGA.text: Your train passes near the Carlton Cinema in Westgate-on-Sea, on the train's {side}. It was built in 1910 as the town hall, but within two years it had become a cinema, and it still shows films today.

MAR-WGA.name: Royal Sea Bathing Hospital
MAR-WGA.text: Your train passes near the Royal Sea Bathing Hospital in Margate, on the train's {side}, founded in 1791 by the Quaker doctor John Coakley Lettsom to treat poor Londoners with scrofula. Its patients were given fresh air, sunshine and sea bathing, and slept on its verandas whenever the weather allowed.

BSR-MAR.name: Scenic Railway, Dreamland
BSR-MAR.text: Your train passes near the Scenic Railway at Dreamland in Margate, on the train's {side}, a wooden roller coaster opened in 1920, with a brakeman riding on each train to control its speed. When it was listed at Grade II* in 2011 it was the oldest working roller coaster in the UK.

BSR-DMP.name: Dickens House Museum, Broadstairs
BSR-DMP.text: Your train passes near the Dickens House Museum in Broadstairs, on the train's {side}. The cottage was the home of Mary Pearson Strong, whom Charles Dickens visited on his family holidays here and who inspired Betsey Trotwood in David Copperfield.

DMP-RAM.name: Montefiore Synagogue
DMP-RAM.text: Your train passes near the Montefiore Synagogue in Ramsgate, on the train's {side}, the private synagogue Sir Moses Montefiore had built on his estate, finished in 1833. He first came to Ramsgate on his honeymoon in 1812, and his mausoleum stands beside it.

RAM-THP.name: St Laurence's Church, Ramsgate
RAM-THP.text: Your train passes near St Laurence's Church, on the train's {side}, founded in 1062 and the oldest church in Ramsgate. After lightning struck it in 1439 it was rebuilt, and its tower raised to the height it is today.

MSR-THP.name: St Augustine's Cross
MSR-THP.text: Your train passes near St Augustine's Cross, on the train's {side}, put up in 1884 to mark Augustine's arrival in England in 597. It's believed to stand where he first met King Ethelbert of Kent.

MSR-STU.name: Minster Abbey
MSR-STU.text: Your train passes near Minster Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in about 670 by the Kentish princess Domne Eafe; legend says her land was as much as her pet deer could mark out in a day. Since 1937 Benedictine nuns have lived here, beside the ruins.

CBW-STU.name: St Dunstan's Church, Canterbury
CBW-STU.text: Your train passes near St Dunstan's Church, on the train's {side}, which dates from the 11th century. In 1174 Henry II changed into sackcloth here before walking to Thomas Becket's tomb in the cathedral, as penance.

CBW-CRT.name: Church of St Mary, Chartham
CBW-CRT.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Chartham, on the train's {side}, begun in about 1285, perhaps with the help of Michael of Canterbury, the master mason at Canterbury Cathedral. Its tower was added in the 14th century.

CIL-CRT.name: Julliberrie's Grave
CIL-CRT.text: Your train passes near Julliberrie's Grave, on the train's {side}, a long barrow probably built in the fourth millennium BC. No human remains have been found in it, but a broken polished stone axe had been placed at its centre.

CIL-WYE.name: Godmersham Park
CIL-WYE.text: Your train passes Godmersham Park, on the train's {side}. Its house, built in 1732, came to Edward Austen Knight, Jane Austen's brother, and she often stayed there.

MSR-SDW.name: Richborough Roman Fort
MSR-SDW.text: Your train passes Richborough Roman Fort, on the train's {side}, whose walls still stand several metres high. As Rutupiae it was a main gateway to Roman Britain after the conquest of AD 43 and the start of Watling Street; the coast is now miles away.

DEA-SDW.name: Deal Castle
DEA-SDW.text: Your train passes near Deal Castle, on the train's {side}, an artillery fort built by Henry VIII in 1539 and 1540 against invasion from France and the Holy Roman Empire. Its moated stone bastions had 66 firing positions for guns.

DEA-WAM.name: Old St Mary's Church, Walmer
DEA-WAM.text: Your train passes near Old St Mary's Church in Upper Walmer, on the train's {side}, built in 1120 as the chapel of Walmer Manor. The Duke of Wellington worshipped here when he stayed at Walmer Castle as Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports, and his hatchment hangs inside.

MTM-WAM.name: Ripple Mill, Ringwould
MTM-WAM.text: Your train passes near Ripple Mill, on the train's {side}, a smock mill first built at Drellingore and moved here in the early 19th century, its corner posts cut in half lengthways and bolted back together. Trinity House once helped pay for repairs, as it was a landmark for ships.

DVP-MTM.name: Maison Dieu, Dover
DVP-MTM.text: Your train passes near the Maison Dieu, on the train's {side}, now the oldest part of Dover Town Hall. Hubert de Burgh, Constable of Dover Castle, founded it in 1203 as a hospital for pilgrims arriving from the Continent on their way to Becket's shrine at Canterbury.

NVN-SEE.name: St John's Church, Piddinghoe
NVN-SEE.text: Your train passes near St John's Church at Piddinghoe, across the River Ouse on the train's {side}. Its round Norman tower is one of three in the Ouse valley, the others being at Southease and St Michael's in Lewes.

NVH-NVN.name: Port of Newhaven
NVH-NVN.text: Your train passes the Port of Newhaven, on the train's {side}, where ferries sail to Dieppe in France. Newhaven was a fishing village of little importance as a port until the railway arrived in 1847.

BIP-NVH.name: Tide Mills
BIP-NVH.text: Your train passes near Tide Mills, on the train's {side}, a village beside a tide mill begun here in 1762. The village was condemned as unfit to live in in 1936 and abandoned in 1939.

BIP-SEF.name: St Leonard's Church, Seaford
BIP-SEF.text: Your train passes near St Leonard's Church, Seaford, on the train's {side}, parts of which are Norman work of the 11th century. In the Middle Ages Seaford was one of the main ports of southern England, but its harbour silted up and the French burned the town several times between 1350 and 1550.

EGH-SNS.name: Staines Railway Bridge
EGH-SNS.text: Your train crosses the River Thames on Staines Railway Bridge, completed in 1856. Its wrought iron girders rest on six cast iron pillars set in the river bed.

SNS-WRY.name: St Mary's Church, Staines
SNS-WRY.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Staines, on the train's {side}, standing on a rise above the Thames at the west end of the town. A plaque on its tower, built in 1631, says it was designed by Inigo Jones.

SNY-WRY.name: Saxon palace site, Old Windsor
SNY-WRY.text: Your train passes near the site of a palace of the Saxon kings at Old Windsor, on the train's {side}. Edward the Confessor held a royal manor here, and the palace was later replaced by the Norman castle at what became Windsor; Old Windsor was the first place to bear the name.

DAT-SNY.name: Datchet Bridge
DAT-SNY.text: Your train passes near where Datchet Bridge crossed the Thames, on the train's {side}. Berkshire and Buckinghamshire argued for decades over its upkeep, and in 1836 each built its own half, one in wood and one in iron, not touching in the middle. It was pulled down in 1848.

DAT-WNR.name: Eton College
DAT-WNR.text: Your train passes Eton College, on the train's {side}, founded by Henry VI in 1440. It is the largest boarding school in England, and has been called "the nurse of England's statesmen".

AFS-SNS.name: HM Prison Bronzefield
AFS-SNS.text: Your train passes HM Prison Bronzefield, on the train's {side}, the largest women's prison in Europe. The site was first a residential school for orphans from London, opened in 1872.

MBK-SOU.name: Mayflower Theatre
MBK-SOU.text: Your train passes near the Mayflower Theatre, on the train's {side}. It opened in 1928 as the Empire, and with seats for 2,300 it is the largest theatre in the south of England outside London.

HYD-KGS.name: St James' Church, Somerton
HYD-KGS.text: Your train passes near St James' Church in Somerton, on the train's {side}. In 1512 the Crown granted the manor to William Fermor, and in the 16th century the church's south aisle became the Fermor family's chapel.

HYD-TAC.name: Rousham House
HYD-TAC.text: Your train passes near Rousham House, on the train's {side}, built in about 1635 and attacked by Parliamentary soldiers in the Civil War. Its gardens were laid out by Charles Bridgeman and then by William Kent.

OXF-TAC.name: Port Meadow
OXF-TAC.text: Your train passes Port Meadow, on the train's {side}, a great stretch of common grazing land beside the Thames. The Freemen of Oxford's right to graze their animals here free of charge is recorded in the Domesday Book, and has been used ever since.

OXF-OXP.name: Radcliffe Observatory
OXF-OXP.text: Your train passes near the Radcliffe Observatory, on the train's {side}, Oxford University's observatory from 1773 until 1934. Its octagonal tower is based on the Tower of the Winds in Athens and is topped by a statue of Atlas holding up the world.

ISP-OXP.name: St Nicholas' Church, Islip
ISP-OXP.text: Your train passes near St Nicholas' Church in Islip, on the train's {side}. Edward the Confessor was born in Islip and baptised in a church here; the font is now at Middleton Stoney.

BIT-ISP.name: Alchester
BIT-ISP.text: Your train crosses the site of Alchester, a Roman town at a crossroads of Roman roads whose Roman name isn't known. Excavations have shown it was one of the earliest legionary fortresses in Britain after the invasion of AD 43.

BIT-HDM.name: Notley Abbey
BIT-HDM.text: Your train passes near the remains of Notley Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded for Augustinian canons in the 12th century and one of the richest in the Oxford area. Laurence Olivier and Vivien Leigh later owned it.

BCS-HDM.name: St Mary's Church, Ludgershall
BCS-HDM.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church in Ludgershall, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church dating from the 14th century. The Bible scholar John Wycliffe is reported to have been one of its early vicars.

BCS-KGS.name: Church of St Peter and St Paul, Kings Sutton
BCS-KGS.text: Your train passes near the church at Kings Sutton, on the train's {side}, whose spire, added in the late 14th century, rises to 198 feet (60 metres). Nikolaus Pevsner thought it "one of the finest, if not the finest, spire in this county of spires".

HDM-PRR.name: St Mary's Church, Haddenham
HDM-PRR.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church in Haddenham, on the train's {side}, of 12th-century Norman origin. Haddenham is one of only three wychert villages in England, with walls built of white clay mixed with straw.

PRR-SDR.name: Church of St Mary and St Nicholas, Saunderton
