PRR-SDR.text: Your train passes near Saunderton's church of St Mary and St Nicholas, on the train's {side}. It took its second saint in 1452, when the village's other church, St Nicholas, was pulled down After its walls began to lean in 1886 it was largely taken down and rebuilt.

MRS-PRR.name: The Mount, Princes Risborough
MRS-PRR.text: Your train passes near The Mount, on the train's {side}, now a car park but once the site of Risborough's royal manor house. The Black Prince was lord of the manor, and after his death the town became known as Prince Risberge, later Princes Risborough.

LTK-MRS.name: St Nicholas' Church, Great Kimble
LTK-MRS.text: Your train passes near St Nicholas' Church in Great Kimble, on the train's {side}. It was in this parish that John Hampden refused to pay his ship money in January 1636.

AYS-LTK.name: All Saints Church, Little Kimble
AYS-LTK.text: Your train passes near All Saints Church in Little Kimble, on the train's {side}. Inside are the remains of early 14th-century wall paintings of saints, among them St Francis preaching to the birds and a large St George.

AVP-AYS.name: Roman settlement at Fleet Marston
AVP-AYS.text: Your train passes the site of a Roman settlement at Fleet Marston, on the train's {side}, on the line of Akeman Street, the Roman road. In 2022 archaeologists working on HS2 found a Roman cemetery in the parish, with about 425 burials and 1,200 coins.

AYS-SKM.name: Stoke Mandeville Stadium
AYS-SKM.text: Your train passes near Stoke Mandeville Stadium, on the train's {side}, the National Centre for Disability Sport. It grew out of the Stoke Mandeville Games, the forerunner of the Paralympic Games, started in 1948 by the neurosurgeon Ludwig Guttmann at the hospital next door.

SKM-WND.name: Stoke Mandeville
SKM-WND.text: Your train passes near the village of Stoke Mandeville, on the train's {side}, whose name comes from the Norman de Mandeville family, first recorded here in 1284. Its old church stood alone a kilometre from the village; excavations for HS2 on its site found two Roman statues.

GMN-WND.name: St Mary's Church, Wendover
GMN-WND.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Wendover, on the train's {side}. Early Wendover seems to have been centred near the church, south of today's town centre; the town was granted a market charter in 1214.

AMR-GMN.name: Gipsy House
AMR-GMN.text: Your train passes near Gipsy House, on the train's {side}, the home of the writer Roald Dahl and his family for several decades. He and his wife, the actor Patricia Neal, bought it at auction for £4,500 in 1954.

AMR-CFO.name: Little Chalfont
AMR-CFO.text: Your train passes Little Chalfont, on the train's {side}, a village that grew up in the 20th century round its station. The station opened in 1889 as Chalfont Road, among isolated farms, and was renamed Chalfont & Latimer in 1915.

CFO-CLW.name: Buckinghamshire and Hertfordshire
CFO-CLW.text: Between Chalfont & Latimer and Chorleywood, your train passes from Buckinghamshire into Hertfordshire.
CFO-CLW.textReverse: Between Chorleywood and Chalfont & Latimer, your train passes from Hertfordshire into Buckinghamshire.

HWY-SDR.name: Hellfire Caves
HWY-SDR.text: Your train passes near the Hellfire Caves, on the train's {side}, man-made chalk and flint caverns running 260 metres into the hill above West Wycombe. They were dug between 1748 and 1752 for Sir Francis Dashwood, co-founder of the Hellfire Club, which met in them.

BCF-HWY.name: Wycombe Abbey
BCF-HWY.text: Your train passes near Wycombe Abbey, on the train's {side}, a girls' boarding school founded in 1896 by Dame Frances Dove. Its grounds of woods, gardens and a lake include a Cold War bunker.

BCF-SRG.name: Bekonscot
BCF-SRG.text: Your train passes near Bekonscot, on the train's {side}, a model village built in the 1920s by Roland Callingham at one inch to one foot, often called the oldest surviving model village in Britain. It helped inspire Enid Blyton.

GER-SRG.name: Jordans Meeting House
GER-SRG.text: Your train passes near Jordans, on the train's {side}, whose Quaker meeting house was built in 1688 and is one of the oldest in the country. William Penn, the founder of Pennsylvania, is buried in its burial ground.

DGC-GER.name: Chalfont Viaduct
DGC-GER.text: Your train crosses the M25 on the Chalfont Viaduct, five brick arches built between 1902 and 1906, long before the motorway passed beneath. A second, longer viaduct just to the west spans the A413.

DGC-DNM.name: Denham Place
DGC-DNM.text: Your train passes near Denham Place, on the train's {side}, a Dutch-style house built between 1688 and 1701 for Sir Roger Hill. Capability Brown landscaped its park in 1773, and later residents included members of the Bonaparte family and the American banker J. P. Morgan.

BIT-BLY.name: Bletchley Park
BIT-BLY.text: Your train passes near Bletchley Park, on the train's {side}, where codebreakers including Alan Turing broke the German Enigma and Lorenz ciphers during the Second World War.

BLY-MKC.name: National Bowl
BLY-MKC.text: Your train passes near the National Bowl, on the train's {side}, an open-air arena made from an old clay pit for brick-making. It opened in 1979; Queen played here in 1982, and Michael Jackson drew 60,000 fans on each of three nights.

MKC-WOL.name: Concrete Cows
MKC-WOL.text: Your train passes near the Concrete Cows, on the train's {side}, the replicas by the line at Bancroft of Liz Leyh's three cows and three calves of 1978. The originals, made from scrap and skinned with concrete, are now at Milton Keynes Museum.

BLY-LBZ.name: Linslade Tunnel
BLY-LBZ.text: Your train runs through Linslade Tunnel, whose three bores are the only tunnel on the London and Birmingham Railway built on a bend: local landowners refused to let the line pass closer to Leighton Buzzard. The first bore opened in 1837.

BLY-FEN.name: St Martin's Church, Fenny Stratford
BLY-FEN.text: Your train passes near St Martin's Church in Fenny Stratford, on the train's {side}, built by Browne Willis, its first stone laid on St Martin's Day 1724. Every St Martin's Day, November 11th, the Fenny Poppers, six small ceremonial cannon, are fired with blank charges at noon, 2pm and 4pm.

BWB-FEN.name: Magiovinium
BWB-FEN.text: Your train passes near the site of Magiovinium, on the train's {side}, a Roman town and fort at Dropshot Farm, at the edge of Fenny Stratford. Two hoards of Roman silver coins were found at or near the site, in 1967 and 1987.

BWB-WOB.name: Red Bull Racing
BWB-WOB.text: Your train passes near the factory of Red Bull Racing, on the train's {side}, the Formula One team based in Milton Keynes since 2004. It won the Constructors' Championship four years running from 2010, with Sebastian Vettel, and again in 2022 and 2023.

CED-LBZ.name: Bridego Bridge
CED-LBZ.text: Your train crosses Bridego Bridge, now officially Mentmore Bridge, where in August 1963 the Great Train Robbers stopped a Royal Mail train from Glasgow to London and escaped with more than £2.6 million. Most of the money was never found.

CED-TRI.name: Tring Cutting
CED-TRI.text: Your train runs through Tring Cutting, two and a half miles long and up to 60 feet deep, on the boundary of Hertfordshire and Buckinghamshire. It was dug for the London and Birmingham Railway, opened in 1837, whose engineer, Robert Stephenson, was determined to keep its gradients as gentle as possible.

LKE-SHN.name: Shanklin
LKE-SHN.text: Your train runs into Shanklin, whose town is on the train's {side}, a seaside resort known for its Old Village and Shanklin Chine, a wooded ravine. The poet John Keats lodged in the High Street in the summer of 1819.

LKE-SAN.name: Sandown Barrack Battery
LKE-SAN.text: Your train passes near Sandown Barrack Battery, on the train's {side}, one of the Palmerston Forts built to defend the Isle of Wight against a feared French invasion. It was built between 1861 and 1863 for £6,233.

BDN-SAN.name: Brading Roman Villa
BDN-SAN.text: Your train passes near Brading Roman Villa, on the train's {side}, found in 1879 when a farmer making holes for a sheep pen struck a mosaic floor. The villa grew around three sides of a courtyard, and its mosaics are on show under a cover building.

BDN-SAB.name: Nunwell House
BDN-SAB.text: Your train passes near Nunwell House, on the train's {side}, home of the Oglander family for centuries. Sir John Oglander, a Royalist, hosted Charles I here on the King's last night of freedom.

RYR-SAB.name: Smallbrook Junction station
RYR-SAB.text: Smallbrook Junction station, at one end of this stretch, can't be reached except by train: it exists only for changing trains between Island Line and the Isle of Wight Steam Railway. It opened in 1991.

RYD-RYR.name: Royal Victoria Arcade
RYD-RYR.text: Your train passes near the Royal Victoria Arcade in Ryde, on the train's {side}, built in 1835 and 1836 and one of the first purpose-built shopping centres. It was named after Princess Victoria, later Queen Victoria, who had stayed at nearby Norris Castle.

RYD-RYP.name: Ryde Pier
RYD-RYP.text: Your train runs along Ryde Pier, the world's oldest seaside pleasure pier, opened in 1814. Before it was built, passengers were carried ashore on a porter's back and might have to walk up to half a mile across wet sand.

SHP-UPH.name: Shepperton station
SHP-UPH.text: Shepperton station, at one end of this stretch, is the terminus of a branch that opened in 1864. It was first meant to carry on to the River Thames by Chertsey Bridge, but that plan was dropped in 1862.

SUU-UPH.name: Upper Halliford station
SUU-UPH.text: Upper Halliford station, at one end of this stretch, opened as a halt in 1944 for a wartime factory of the British Thermostat Company that made munitions. Its second platform followed in 1946.

KMP-SUU.name: Kempton Park
KMP-SUU.text: Your train passes Kempton Park, on the train's {side}, first enclosed as a royal park in 1246; Henry VIII later hunted here. It is now home to Kempton Park Racecourse and a nature reserve.

HMP-KMP.name: Kempton Park Steam Engines
HMP-KMP.text: Your train passes near the Kempton Park waterworks, on the train's {side}, home to two triple-expansion steam engines of the late 1920s that each weigh more than 800 tons. One, the Sir William Prescott, still runs: the largest working engine of its kind in the world.

TAD-TAT.name: Tattenham Corner
TAD-TAT.text: Your train passes near Tattenham Corner, on the train's {side}, the sharp bend at the top of Epsom Racecourse and the last before the home straight of the Derby. Queen Elizabeth II used to arrive at the station by Royal Train on race days.

KND-TAD.name: Tadworth Court
KND-TAD.text: Your train passes near Tadworth Court, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed house built in 1700 in the Queen Anne style for Leonard Wessels, lord of the manor of Banstead. It is now home to The Children's Trust, a charity for disabled children.

CHP-KND.name: Fames Rough
CHP-KND.text: Your train passes near Fames Rough, on the train's {side}, a Surrey Wildlife Trust reserve on the Chipstead Downs. Part of its grassland is ploughed now and then to give a home to three very rare plants of arable fields, among them ground pine.

CHP-WME.name: Woodmansterne station
CHP-WME.text: Woodmansterne station, at one end of this stretch, isn't in Woodmansterne: the village lies across the Greater London boundary in Surrey, while the station serves the western side of Coulsdon.

BAD-EPD.name: Epsom College
BAD-EPD.text: Your train passes near Epsom College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1853 as the Royal Medical Benevolent College, to house pensioned doctors and to educate the sons of poor or deceased doctors.

BAD-BLM.name: Gally Hills, Banstead Downs
BAD-BLM.text: Your train passes near the Gally Hills on Banstead Downs, on the train's {side}, where Saxon burial mounds survive. Bronze Age axes and Iron Age and Roman pottery have also been found on the downs.

CDN-ELD.name: Farthing Downs
CDN-ELD.text: Your train passes near Farthing Downs, on the train's {side}, the largest area of semi-natural downland left in Greater London, owned by the City of London Corporation. Early medieval burial mounds survive at its north end.

ELD-SAF.name: East Surrey Hospital
ELD-SAF.text: Your train passes near East Surrey Hospital, on the train's {side}, which began as Reigate Cottage Hospital in 1866. The present hospital opened in 1981 and was formally opened by Margaret Thatcher in 1984.

HOR-SAF.name: Archway Theatre
HOR-SAF.text: Your train passes the Archway Theatre in Horley, on the train's {side}, an amateur theatre under the railway arches of the Victoria Road bridge, built in 1909. It has a 95-seat main auditorium and stages ten main productions a year.

WHS-WHY.name: RAF Kenley
WHS-WHY.text: Your train passes near the old airfield of RAF Kenley, on the train's {side}, one of the three RAF stations given the defence of London in the Battle of Britain. Pens built to shelter its fighters still survive.

CAT-WHS.name: Caterham Cars
CAT-WHS.text: Your train passes the former home of Caterham Cars, on the train's {side}, beside Caterham station. The firm bought the rights to the Lotus Seven in 1973 and still makes the Caterham Seven; its factory was in Caterham until 1987 and its showroom here until 2013.

UWL-WOH.name: Woldingham station
UWL-WOH.text: Woldingham station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1885 as Marden Park, named after the nearby manor, a year after the line itself. It was renamed Woldingham in 1894.

OXT-WOH.name: Oxted Tunnel
OXT-WOH.text: Your train runs through Oxted Tunnel, more than a mile long. It was dug in the 1860s, but work on the line stopped in 1869 and it did not open until 1884.

HUR-OXT.name: Limpsfield Tunnel
HUR-OXT.text: Your train runs through Limpsfield Tunnel, 551 yards long, at the southern end of Oxted station. The line through it opened in 1884.

HUR-LFD.name: St Peter and St Paul's Church, Lingfield
HUR-LFD.text: Your train passes near the church of St Peter and St Paul in Lingfield, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in 1431. Its brasses and monuments, including the tomb of Reginald de Cobham, 1st Baron Cobham, are among the finest in England.

DMS-LFD.name: Lingfield Park Racecourse
DMS-LFD.text: Your train passes Lingfield Park Racecourse, on the train's {side}, best known for flat racing in winter on an all-weather Polytrack rather than turf. Lingfield station adjoins the course.

DMS-EGR.name: Queen Victoria Hospital
DMS-EGR.text: Your train passes near the Queen Victoria Hospital in East Grinstead, on the train's {side}, where in the Second World War Archibald McIndoe pioneered reconstructive surgery for badly burned airmen. His patients formed the Guinea Pig Club here in 1941.

EBT-HUR.name: Eden Valley Museum
EBT-HUR.text: Your train passes near the Eden Valley Museum in Edenbridge, on the train's {side}, in a medieval farmhouse. Its collections include cricket-ball making, and a needlework box made by a German prisoner of war that featured in the BBC's A History of the World in 100 Objects.

EBT-HEV.name: St Peter and St Paul's Church, Edenbridge
EBT-HEV.text: Your train passes near the church of St Peter and St Paul in Edenbridge, on the train's {side}, whose oldest walls date from the 11th or early 12th century. Inside is stained glass by Edward Burne-Jones.

CWN-HEV.name: Markbeech
CWN-HEV.text: Your train passes near Markbeech, on the train's {side}, a small village on the northern ridges of the High Weald, in the parish of Hever, whose castle was the childhood home of Anne Boleyn.

AHS-CWN.name: Cowden Meadow
AHS-CWN.text: Your train passes Cowden Meadow, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest whose grassland has not been cultivated for many years, so it keeps flowers such as quaking grass, oxeye daisy and pepper saxifrage.

AHS-ERI.name: Harrison's Rocks
AHS-ERI.text: Your train passes near Harrison's Rocks, on the train's {side}, a line of sandstone crags in the woods south of Groombridge. Climbers own them, through the British Mountaineering Council since 2009, and the soft rock has about 400 short climbs, all done on a top rope.

COH-ERI.name: Jarvis Brook
COH-ERI.text: Your train passes near Jarvis Brook, on the train's {side}, the village where Crowborough station actually stands; the village grew when the station opened. Its brickworks closed in 1980, and the quarry that fed them became a local nature reserve in 2009.

BXD-COH.name: Iron furnace near Buxted
BXD-COH.text: Your train passes near the remains of an iron furnace, on the train's {side}, a scheduled monument from the days when the Weald made England's iron. Buxted was at the heart of it: the first cast-iron cannon made in England was cast near the village in 1543, by Ralf Hogge.

BXD-UCK.name: Buxted
BXD-UCK.text: Your train passes near Buxted, on the train's {side}. In the early 1800s the Prime Minister Lord Liverpool bought Buxted Park and enlarged it, pressing the villagers to leave their houses: by 1836 the old village centre had gone, and only its church stayed in the park.

RDG-TLH.name: Chazey Court Barn
RDG-TLH.text: Your train passes near Chazey Court Barn, on the train's {side} across the Thames: a huge seven-bay brick barn from about 1700, listed Grade I.

ANG-LIT.name: Littlehampton
ANG-LIT.text: Your train passes near Littlehampton, on the train's {side}, a fishing town at the mouth of the Arun that became a port and resort, with a ferry across the Channel to Honfleur. Its population grew tenfold in the 1800s, from 584 in 1801 to 5,954 in 1901.

ARU-LIT.name: Littlehampton Lifeboat Station
ARU-LIT.text: Your train passes near Littlehampton Lifeboat Station, on the train's {side}, on the east bank of the Arun. The RNLI opened a station here in 1884; its inshore lifeboat of 1967 was paid for by an appeal on BBC TV's Blue Peter and named Blue Peter I.

ASN-BFN.name: London Bus Museum
ASN-BFN.text: Your train passes near the London Bus Museum at Brooklands, on the train's {side}. About 35 of its buses and coaches are on show, from Victorian horse-drawn omnibuses to Routemasters, including the only surviving wartime utility bus that ran in London.

SDW-THP.name: White Mill, Sandwich
SDW-THP.text: Your train passes near White Mill, on the train's {side}, a smock mill west of Sandwich built in 1760. It last worked by wind in 1926 and by an oil engine until 1957, and is now a rural heritage centre, with the miller's cottage furnished as it was between 1900 and 1939.

DNM-WRU.name: Harefield Road
DNM-WRU.text: Your train passes the site of Harefield Road, a station planned in the late 1930s for the Central line's extension to Denham. The war stopped the work, and afterwards the green belt ruled out the new houses it was meant to serve, so it was never built.

SRU-WRU.name: RAF West Ruislip
SRU-WRU.text: Your train passes the site of RAF West Ruislip, on the train's {side}, a depot chosen in 1917 for the Royal Flying Corps and split in two by this line. The US Air Force took it over in 1955 and the US Navy in 1975; after the Navy left in 2006 it was cleared for housing.

NLT-SRU.name: RAF South Ruislip
NLT-SRU.text: Your train passes the site of RAF South Ruislip, on the train's {side}, the headquarters of the US Air Force's Third Air Force from 1949 to 1972. In 1970 three teenagers whose fathers were stationed here, Dewey Bunnell, Dan Peek and Gerry Beckley, formed the band America.

NLT-SDH.name: Orley Farm School
NLT-SDH.text: Your train passes near Orley Farm School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1850 to prepare boys for Harrow School. In 1862 it took its name from Anthony Trollope's novel Orley Farm, which describes the buildings and grounds the Trollope family once owned and the school later used.

SDH-SUD.name: Sudbury Town Underground station
SDH-SUD.text: Your train passes near Sudbury Town Underground station, on the train's {side}, rebuilt by Charles Holden in brick, concrete and glass in the early 1930s. It first opened in 1903, on the first of the Underground's surface lines to run electric trains instead of steam.

SUD-WCX.name: Wembley Stadium
SUD-WCX.text: Your train passes near Wembley Stadium, on the train's {side}, England's national football stadium, opened in 2007 where the old Wembley stood from 1923 to 2000. With 90,000 seats it is the largest stadium in the UK, and its arch carries more than three quarters of the roof's weight.

MYB-WCX.name: Lord's Cricket Ground
MYB-WCX.text: Your train passes near Lord's Cricket Ground, on the train's {side}, the third ground Thomas Lord opened, in 1814: his second had to go when the Regent's Canal was cut through its outfield. The pitch has a pronounced slope, running down from north to south.

HOH-MYB.name: Abbey Road Studios
HOH-MYB.text: Your train passes near Abbey Road Studios, on the train's {side}, opened by the Gramophone Company in November 1931 behind a Georgian townhouse. The Beatles were its most famous clients, working mostly in Studio Two, and the building was listed in 2010 when it was under threat of sale.

HOH-RIC.name: The More
HOH-RIC.text: Your train passes near the site of The More, on the train's {side}, a palace owned by Cardinal Wolsey and then Henry VIII, where Catherine of Aragon lived in the winter of 1531 to 1532. In 1527 the French ambassador thought it more splendid than Hampton Court; nothing now remains above ground.

HWV-HXX.name: Heathrow Terminal 5
HWV-HXX.text: Your train passes near Heathrow Terminal 5, on the train's {side}, opened in 2008 after the longest public inquiry in British history. Its main building, designed by the Richard Rogers Partnership, is the largest free-standing structure in the UK.

HAF-HXX.name: Heathrow Terminal 4
HAF-HXX.text: Your train passes near Heathrow Terminal 4, on the train's {side}, built for £200 million south of the southern runway and opened by the Prince and Princess of Wales on April 1st 1986. British Airways was based here until 2009, when it moved to the airport's newest terminal.

HAY-HXX.name: Heathrow Terminal 1
HAY-HXX.text: Your train passes near Heathrow Terminal 1, on the train's {side}, designed by Frederick Gibberd and opened by Queen Elizabeth II in April 1969, when it was the largest new airport terminal in western Europe. It closed in 2015 to make way for a bigger Terminal 2.

HAY-STL.name: Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha
HAY-STL.text: Your train passes near Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha, on the train's {side}. When it opened in 2003, Guinness World Records named it the largest Sikh temple outside India.

HAN-STL.name: Wharncliffe Viaduct
HAN-STL.text: Your train crosses the Wharncliffe Viaduct over the Brent valley, Isambard Kingdom Brunel's first major design for the railway, built in 1836 and 1837. Lord Wharncliffe's coat of arms is carved on its south side.

AFS-FEL.name: Bedfont Lakes Country Park
AFS-FEL.text: Your train passes near Bedfont Lakes Country Park, on the train's {side}, 72.5 hectares of lakes, meadows and woodland. Gravel was dug here from the 1860s and it was a landfill site until 1973; it became a nature reserve in 2000, and is home to 156 species of bird.

FEL-WTN.name: Feltham marshalling yard
FEL-WTN.text: Your train passes the site of Feltham marshalling yard, on the train's {side}, a hump yard built with the help of about 200 German prisoners of war and opened in 1918 to sort freight for south-west London. It closed in 1969, and part of the site is being rebuilt to stable South Western Railway's trains.

FEL-HOU.name: Hounslow Heath
FEL-HOU.text: Your train passes near Hounslow Heath, on the train's {side}, all that remains of a heath that once spread across Feltham, Hounslow, Twickenham and what is now Heathrow. Armies camped on it, Cromwell's in 1647 among them, and in the 17th and 18th centuries it was notorious for highwaymen.

HOU-ISL.name: Worton Hall (Isleworth Studios)
HOU-ISL.text: Your train passes near Worton Hall, on the train's {side}, a house of 1783 that became a film studio in 1914. Alexander Korda made Things to Come here in 1936, from H. G. Wells's screenplay; the studios closed in 1952.

HOU-WTN.name: Whitton Park
HOU-WTN.text: Your train passes near the site of Whitton Park, on the train's {side}, the estate of the 3rd Duke of Argyll, whom Horace Walpole nicknamed the Treemonger. After his death in 1761 many of his trees went to the Princess of Wales's new garden at Kew; a black locust planted there in 1762 still survives.

TWI-WTN.name: All Hallows, Twickenham
TWI-WTN.text: Your train passes near All Hallows church, on the train's {side}, which has the tower of Wren's All Hallows Lombard Street. When that City church was demolished in 1937, its tower, bells, cloister and many fittings were moved here, and a new church was built around them.

STW-TWI.name: Strawberry Hill House
STW-TWI.text: Your train passes near Strawberry Hill House, on the train's {side}, the Gothic villa Horace Walpole built up in stages from 1749 to suit his collection of antiquities. Its style, Strawberry Hill Gothic, foreshadowed the Victorian Gothic Revival.

FLW-STW.name: Fulwell bus garage
FLW-STW.text: Your train passes near Fulwell bus garage, on the train's {side}, built in 1902 and 1903 as a tram depot for London United Tramways. London's first trolleybuses arrived here in 1931, and it later became London Transport's main trolleybus works.

FLW-HMP.name: Bushy Park
FLW-HMP.text: Your train passes near Bushy Park, on the train's {side}, the second largest of London's Royal Parks, which Henry VIII made a deer-hunting ground. In the Second World War General Eisenhower planned the D-Day landings from his headquarters in the park, and herds of red and fallow deer still live here.

SMG-TWI.name: Sandycombe Lodge
SMG-TWI.text: Your train passes near Sandycombe Lodge, on the train's {side}, the country retreat J. M. W. Turner designed and built in 1813 and lived in from 1814 to 1826. It is the only surviving building he designed.

RMD-SMG.name: Richmond Railway Bridge
RMD-SMG.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Richmond Railway Bridge, one of the first railway bridges over the river, opened in 1848 to Joseph Locke's design. Doubts about its cast iron led to a rebuilding in steel from 1906 to 1908, keeping much of the original look.

KWG-RMD.name: Palm House, Kew Gardens
KWG-RMD.text: Your train passes near the Palm House at Kew Gardens, on the train's {side}, finished in 1848 and the first greenhouse built on such a scale. It was also the first large-scale use of wrought iron in a building, and many of its tropical plants are endangered or extinct in the wild.

NSH-RMD.name: Crawdaddy Club
NSH-RMD.text: Your train passes near the Station Hotel, on the train's {side}, whose back room became the Crawdaddy Club in 1963. The Rolling Stones were its house band in its first year, followed by the Yardbirds; the club took its name from Bo Diddley's song Doing the Craw-Daddy.

MTL-NSH.name: Mortlake Brewery
MTL-NSH.text: Your train passes near Mortlake Brewery, on the train's {side}, where brewing is recorded as early as 1487. As it grew in the 1850s it supplied India Pale Ale to the British army in India, and it brewed Budweiser from 1995 to 2011, before closing in 2015.

BNS-MTL.name: Mausoleum of Sir Richard and Lady Burton
BNS-MTL.text: Your train passes near the tomb of the explorer Sir Richard Burton, on the train's {side}, a mausoleum of marble and stone shaped like a tent, designed by his wife Isabel. Their coffins can be seen through a glass panel at the back.

BNI-BNS.name: The Bull's Head, Barnes
BNI-BNS.text: Your train passes near the Bull's Head, on the train's {side}, a riverside pub in Barnes, rebuilt in 1846, that opened as a jazz venue in 1959. It became one of the most important jazz venues in Britain, known as the suburban Ronnie Scott's.

BNI-CHK.name: Barnes Railway Bridge
BNI-CHK.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Barnes Railway Bridge, first opened in 1849 to Joseph Locke's design; it also carries a footpath. It is a landmark of the Boat Race, and its coat of arms has a light blue oar for Cambridge and a dark blue oar for Oxford.

CHK-KWB.name: Q Theatre
CHK-KWB.text: Your train passes the site of the Q Theatre, on the train's {side}, by Kew Bridge, which put on new plays from 1924 to 1958. Vivien Leigh, Dirk Bogarde and Joan Collins began their stage careers here, and it staged Terence Rattigan's first plays.

BFD-KWB.name: London Museum of Water & Steam
BFD-KWB.text: Your train passes near the London Museum of Water & Steam, on the train's {side}, in Kew Bridge Pumping Station, opened in 1838 to supply west London with drinking water. It has the world's largest collection of Cornish engines, including the largest surviving single-cylinder beam engine in the world.

BFD-SYL.name: Firestone Tyre Factory
BFD-SYL.text: Your train passes the site of the Firestone Tyre Factory, on the train's {side}, an Art Deco landmark on the Great West Road opened in 1928. It was demolished over the August bank holiday in 1980, reportedly before it could be listed, which led to the listing of 150 interwar buildings; its gates and railings survive.

ISL-SYL.name: Brentford & Isleworth Meeting House
ISL-SYL.text: Your train passes near the Quaker meeting house in Isleworth, on the train's {side}, built in 1785 on land bought for £35. It is one of the oldest purpose-built meeting houses in London, with a Quaker burial ground and a garden around it.

BNS-PUT.name: The Pines, Putney
BNS-PUT.text: Your train passes near The Pines, on the train's {side}, a house on Putney Hill where the poet Algernon Charles Swinburne lived with his friend Theodore Watts-Dunton until his death in 1909. Max Beerbohm, who often visited, described it as 'but a few steps from the railway-station'.

PUT-WNT.name: Surrey Iron Railway
PUT-WNT.text: Your train passes near where the Surrey Iron Railway began, on the train's {side}, at a dock on the Thames at Wandsworth. From 1803 its horse-drawn wagons carried coal, lime and building materials about nine miles to Croydon, until it closed in 1846.

CLJ-WNT.name: The Falcon, Battersea
CLJ-WNT.text: Your train passes near the Falcon, on the train's {side}, a pub on St John's Hill recorded as an inn in 1733; the present building dates from 1882 to 1883. The Campaign for Real Ale describes its curved bar counter as the longest in Britain.

CLJ-EAD.name: Wandsworth Common Windmill
CLJ-EAD.text: Your train passes Wandsworth Common Windmill, on the train's {side}, a small smock mill built in 1837 to drain water from this railway's cutting. It pumped the water into an ornamental lake on the common called the Black Sea, and stopped work after the lake was filled in around 1884.

EAD-WIM.name: Wimbledon Traincare Depot
EAD-WIM.text: Your train passes Wimbledon Traincare Depot, on the train's {side}, where South Western Railway's trains are looked after. Opened in 1974, it is one of the busiest depots in the country, with about 250 carriages maintained here each night.

RAY-WIM.name: New Wimbledon Theatre
RAY-WIM.text: Your train passes near the New Wimbledon Theatre, on the train's {side}, an Edwardian theatre that opened on Boxing Day 1910 with the pantomime Jack and Jill. Lionel Bart's Oliver! had its world premiere here in 1960, and it seems to have been the only British theatre with a Turkish bath in the basement.

NEM-RAY.name: New Malden War Memorial
NEM-RAY.text: Your train passes near New Malden's war memorial, on the train's {side}, a three-tiered cenotaph in the High Street unveiled in 1924 by a soldier who had been blinded in the First World War. It was slightly damaged in 1940 when a bomb fell close by during the Blitz.

NBT-NEM.name: Kingsmeadow
NBT-NEM.text: Your train passes near Kingsmeadow, on the train's {side}, a football ground built by Kingstonian in 1989. AFC Wimbledon played here from 2002 until 2020, and it is now the home ground of Chelsea Women.

KNG-NBT.name: Lovekyn Chapel
KNG-NBT.text: Your train passes near the Lovekyn Chapel, on the train's {side}, founded by Edward Lovekyn in 1309, with later gifts from his son John and from William Walworth. It is still used by Kingston Grammar School, whose roots go back to at least the 13th century.

HMW-KNG.name: Kingston Railway Bridge
HMW-KNG.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Kingston Railway Bridge, built in 1907 to replace a cast-iron bridge of 1863. Three of its five arches span the river, and the other two are over dry land.

HMW-TED.name: Normansfield Hospital
HMW-TED.text: Your train passes near Normansfield, on the train's {side}, opened in 1868 by Dr John Langdon Down, after whom Down syndrome is named, as a home for children with learning disabilities. Its Victorian theatre opened in 1879, and the building now houses the Langdon Down Museum of Learning Disability.

BRS-NEM.name: New Malden High Street
BRS-NEM.text: Your train passes near New Malden High Street, on the train's {side}, known for its many Korean shops and restaurants: New Malden has the largest community of South Koreans in Europe.

BRS-SUR.name: Surbiton station
BRS-SUR.text: Surbiton station, at one end of this stretch, was rebuilt in 1937 in an Art Deco style designed by James Robb Scott, and has been called one of the finest modernist stations in Britain. It appears in the very first episode of ITV's Agatha Christie's Poirot.

MOT-RAY.name: Raynes Park station
MOT-RAY.text: Raynes Park station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1871. Its platforms aren't opposite each other, so its long footbridge crosses the four main-line tracks at an angle.

MAL-MOT.name: Malden Manor
MAL-MOT.text: Your train passes near the manor house of Malden, on the train's {side}, beside St John's church and mentioned in the Domesday Book. In 1264 Walter de Merton founded a college here, which later moved to Oxford as Merton College.

MAL-TOL.name: Tolworth Tower
MAL-TOL.text: Your train passes near Tolworth Tower, on the train's {side}, a 22-storey office block 81 metres high beside the Kingston bypass, opened in 1964. The supermarket on its ground floor, first a Fine Fare, was the largest in England when it opened.

CSN-TOL.name: Corinthian-Casuals F.C.
CSN-TOL.text: Your train passes near the ground of Corinthian-Casuals, on the train's {side}, an amateur club formed in 1939 by joining Corinthian, founded in 1882, with Casuals. On a tour of Brazil in the 1988 to 1989 season they played Corinthians, and Sócrates turned out for both teams.

CSN-CSS.name: St Mary the Virgin's Church, Chessington
CSN-CSS.text: Your train passes near St Mary the Virgin's Church in Chessington, on the train's {side}, whose chancel dates from the 12th century; a chapel here is mentioned in Merton Priory's records from 1174 to 1189. When the plaster ceiling was taken down in its Victorian restoration, the date 1636 was found and the old chestnut roof revealed.

MOT-WCP.name: Sir Joseph Hood Memorial Wood
MOT-WCP.text: Your train passes near Sir Joseph Hood Memorial Wood, on the train's {side}, a small nature reserve of oaks planted in the middle of the 19th century, probably as cover for hunting. It is named after Sir Joseph Hood, a former MP and Mayor of Wimbledon.

WBO-WIM.name: Elm Grove tube station
WBO-WIM.text: Your train passes the site of Elm Grove, on the train's {side}, a station also called Tennis Ground that was planned beside the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club's original grounds, for a line approved in 1910 on which the District Railway was to run trains. In the end the Southern Railway built this line, and the station was never built.

SMO-WBO.name: Rutlish School
SMO-WBO.text: Your train passes near Rutlish School, on the train's {side}, named after William Rutlish, embroiderer to Charles II, who left £400 when he died in 1687 to educate poor children of the parish. John Major, Prime Minister from 1990 to 1997, was a pupil at the school.

MDS-SMO.name: Baitul Futuh Mosque
MDS-SMO.text: Your train passes Baitul Futuh, on the train's {side}, one of the largest mosque complexes in Europe, completed in 2003 for the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community. Paid for entirely by donations, it can hold 13,000 worshippers.

MDS-SIH.name: St Lawrence Church, Morden
MDS-SIH.text: Your train passes near St Lawrence Church, on the train's {side}, Morden's parish church, built in 1636 at the highest point of Morden, overlooking Morden Park. It is listed at Grade I.

SIH-SUC.name: Pyl Brook
SIH-SUC.text: Your train passes near the Pyl Brook, on the train's {side}, a small stream that rises in Sutton Common and flows through Merton to join the Beverley Brook in New Malden. Its name probably comes from the Old English pyll, a pool or small stream.

SUC-WSU.name: Gander Green Lane
SUC-WSU.text: Your train passes Gander Green Lane, on the train's {side}, the home ground of Sutton United. On January 7th 1989 Sutton beat Coventry City, then in the top division, by two goals to one here, one of the biggest upsets in FA Cup history.

SUO-WSU.name: The Messenger (David Wynne sculpture)
SUO-WSU.text: Your train passes The Messenger, on the train's {side}, a life-size bronze by David Wynne of a horse and a young rider, put up beside Sutton station in 1981. The rider raises one hand as if calling out, and the horse looks towards the station.

CHE-SUO.name: Whitehall, Cheam
CHE-SUO.text: Your train passes near Whitehall, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed house in Cheam village thought to have been built around 1500 as a yeoman farmer's house. It is now a museum, with a room about Henry VIII's nearby Nonsuch Palace.

BLM-SUO.name: Belmont Pastures
BLM-SUO.text: Your train passes Belmont Pastures, on the train's {side}, a narrow strip of old meadow beside the line that once belonged to Belmont Hospital. Now a nature reserve, its chalk grassland has wild flowers such as bladder campion and knapweed, and grasshoppers and crickets.

CSH-SUO.name: Carshalton House
CSH-SUO.text: Your train passes near Carshalton House, on the train's {side}, built around 1710 for a tobacco merchant who went bankrupt a few years later. In its grounds a water tower of about 1721 pumped water to the house and fountains, and has a bathroom still lined with Delft tiles; the house is now St Philomena's School.

CSB-SUO.name: The Cock sign
CSB-SUO.text: Your train passes near the Cock sign, on the train's {side}, which stands over a crossroads in Sutton High Street. It was put up in 1907 as the sign of the Cock Hotel, later became a road sign and lamp post, and was listed in 2018.

CSB-WLT.name: Carshalton Park
CSB-WLT.text: Your train passes near Carshalton Park, on the train's {side}, now about a tenth of its original size, as the rest was sold for housing from 1892. There were deer in the park until 1898.

WDO-WLT.name: Waddon Ponds
WDO-WLT.text: Your train passes near Waddon Ponds, on the train's {side}, one of the sources of the River Wandle and one of very few places in Croydon where the river can be seen above ground.

WCY-WDO.name: Croydon Palace
WCY-WDO.text: Your train passes near Croydon Palace, on the train's {side}, the summer residence of the Archbishops of Canterbury for more than 500 years, where Henry III and Elizabeth I were regular visitors. From 1889 to 2025 it was a girls' school.

SRS-WCY.name: Croydon Common Athletic Ground
SRS-WCY.text: Your train passes the site of the Nest, on the train's {side}, home ground of Croydon Common from 1908 to 1917 and of Crystal Palace from 1918 to 1924. A train depot now stands on the site, and the ground's front wall still stands along Selhurst Road.

SRS-TTH.name: BRIT School
SRS-TTH.text: Your train passes near the BRIT School, on the train's {side}, a school for the performing and creative arts, free to attend, that opened in 1991. Adele and Amy Winehouse are among its former pupils.

NRB-TTH.name: J. W. Hobbs' Ground
NRB-TTH.text: Your train passes near the site of J. W. Hobbs' Ground, on the train's {side}, a cricket ground laid out in 1885 in the grounds of Norbury Hall. Its only first-class match was against the touring Australians in 1888, and cricket went on here until a leisure centre was built on it in the 1990s.

NRB-SRC.name: Norbury Estate
NRB-SRC.text: Your train passes near the Norbury Estate, on the train's {side}, a London County Council cottage estate built from 1901 to 1920 and influenced by the garden city movement. It stands on an old brickfield, whose clay was fired to make bricks for the estate.

BAL-SRC.name: Tooting Bec Lido
BAL-SRC.text: Your train passes Tooting Bec Lido, on the train's {side}, opened in 1906 and the largest freshwater swimming pool by surface area in the UK, 100 yards long and 33 yards wide. Brad Pitt's pool scene in the film Snatch was shot here.

BAL-WSW.name: Chez Bruce
BAL-WSW.text: Your train passes near Chez Bruce, on the train's {side}, a restaurant opened in 1995 that has held a Michelin star since 1999. It is on the site of Harveys, Marco Pierre White's former restaurant.

CLJ-WSW.name: Royal Victoria Patriotic Building
CLJ-WSW.text: Your train passes near the Royal Victoria Patriotic Building, on the train's {side}, built in 1859 beside Wandsworth Common as a school for girls orphaned in the Crimean War. In the Second World War it became the London Reception Centre, where 34,000 people arriving from occupied Europe were questioned to find spies among them.

CLJ-IMW.name: Battersea Railway Bridge
CLJ-IMW.text: Your train crosses the Thames on Battersea Railway Bridge, dating from 1863 and one of the oldest crossings of the river in London. It was first called the Cremorne Bridge, after the Cremorne pleasure gardens in Chelsea, and once carried broad-gauge track for Great Western trains to Victoria.

IMW-WBP.name: Stamford Bridge
IMW-WBP.text: Your train passes near Stamford Bridge, on the train's {side}, home of Chelsea since the club was founded in 1905. The ground opened in 1877 for the London Athletic Club, and its record crowd, 82,905, came to see Chelsea play Arsenal in 1935.

KPA-WBP.name: Earls Court Exhibition Centre
KPA-WBP.text: Your train passes the site of the Earls Court Exhibition Centre, on the train's {side}, an art moderne hall built between 1935 and 1937. For decades it hosted the Royal Tournament, the Ideal Home Show and Crufts, and events of the 1948 Olympics; its demolition was finished in 2017.

KPA-SPB.name: Olympia
KPA-SPB.text: Your train passes near Olympia, on the train's {side}, which opened in 1886, built as the National Agricultural Hall. Its Grand Hall, with an iron roof made by Handyside of Derby, is listed at Grade II*.

SPB-WIJ.name: White City Stadium
SPB-WIJ.text: Your train passes near the site of White City Stadium, on the train's {side}, built in 10 months for the 1908 Olympics and demolished in 1985. The Olympic marathon finished there, and the race's distance was fixed at those Games, measured from a start at Windsor Castle.

WIJ-WMB.name: Stonebridge Park power station
WIJ-WMB.text: Your train passes near the site of Stonebridge Park power station, on the train's {side}, built in 1913 to 1914 by the London and North Western Railway. From 1914 until 1967 it made the electricity for the suburban electric trains between Euston and Watford.

NWB-WMB.name: Hirst Research Centre
NWB-WMB.text: Your train passes near the Hirst Research Centre, on the train's {side}, set up by the General Electric Company and formally opened in 1923 as one of the first specialised industrial research laboratories built in Britain. In the Second World War its engineers made the cavity magnetron far more powerful, helping to make radar small enough to fit in fighter aircraft.

NWB-SOK.name: The Windermere, South Kenton
NWB-SOK.text: Your train passes near the Windermere, on the train's {side}, a pub built in about 1938 and listed at Grade II. Its interior is on the Campaign for Real Ale's National Inventory of Historic Pub Interiors.

KNT-SOK.name: Northwick Park
KNT-SOK.text: Your train passes near Northwick Park, on the train's {side}, for centuries part of Sheepcote Farm in the manor of Harrow. The land passed to Harrow School, and in the 1930s Middlesex County Council bought 192 acres of it from the school for a public park.

HRW-KNT.name: Harrow Skate Park
HRW-KNT.text: Your train passes near Harrow Skate Park, on the train's {side}, opened on July 15th 1978. It is one of only two concrete skateparks from the 1970s still in use in Britain, and its pool was modelled on one in Spring Valley, California.

HDL-HRW.name: Kodak Harrow works
HDL-HRW.text: Your train passes near Kodak's former Harrow works, on the train's {side}, opened in 1891 as the company's first factory outside the United States. At its peak in the mid-20th century it employed up to 6,000 people; film-making ended in 2005 and the plant closed in 2016.

HDL-HTE.name: Hatch End station
HDL-HTE.text: Your train passes Hatch End station, rebuilt in 1911 to a design by the architect Gerald Horsley. It opened as Pinner, and took its present name in 1956; Bakerloo line trains called here from 1917 until 1982.

SBP-WMB.name: Wembley Central Mosque
SBP-WMB.text: Your train passes near Wembley Central Mosque, on the train's {side}, built in 1904 as St Andrew's Presbyterian Church, in a style influenced by the Arts and Crafts movement. With the Muslim Welfare Association next door, it can hold up to 2,200 people.

HDN-SBP.name: Ace Cafe
HDN-SBP.text: Your train passes near the Ace Cafe, on the train's {side}, opened in 1938 for traffic on the new North Circular Road and famous in motorcycle culture. It closed in 1969 and reopened on the same site in 1997.

HDN-WIJ.name: Our Lady of Willesden Church
HDN-WIJ.text: Your train passes near Our Lady of Willesden Church, on the train's {side}, a Catholic church built from 1929 to 1931 in the Romanesque Revival style. It houses a shrine to Our Lady of Willesden, whose statue dates from 1892.

ACC-WIJ.name: Park Ward works
ACC-WIJ.text: Your train passes near the former works of Park Ward, on the train's {side}, a coachbuilder founded in 1919 that made car bodies for Bentley and Rolls-Royce. Rolls-Royce bought it in 1939, and in 1961 it merged with H. J. Mulliner to become Mulliner Park Ward.

ACC-SAT.name: Eden Studios
ACC-SAT.text: Your train passes near where Eden Studios stood, on the train's {side}, a recording studio in Beaumont Road, Chiswick, from 1972 until it closed in 2007. Elvis Costello, Madness, the Smiths and Kylie Minogue are among those who recorded there; the site was then cleared for housing.

GUN-SAT.name: Gunnersbury Triangle
GUN-SAT.text: Your train passes near Gunnersbury Triangle, on the train's {side}, a patch of woodland hemmed in by three railway lines. In 1983 it became the first place in Britain where a public inquiry stopped building because of the land's value for nature, and it opened as a nature reserve in 1985.

GUN-KWG.name: The National Archives
GUN-KWG.text: Your train passes near the National Archives at Kew, on the train's {side}, the UK government's official archive, whose first building here was opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 1977. Its records span 1,000 years, from Domesday Book to the present, and the site was once a First World War hospital.

KNL-WIJ.name: Kensal Green Cemetery
KNL-WIJ.text: Your train passes near Kensal Green Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1833 and one of London's 'Magnificent Seven' cemeteries. Among those buried there are the engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel and the novelists William Makepeace Thackeray and Anthony Trollope.

KNR-WIJ.name: Kensal Rise Library
KNR-WIJ.text: Your train passes near Kensal Rise Library, on the train's {side}, opened by Mark Twain in 1900 on land given by All Souls College, Oxford. When it was threatened with closure, Alan Bennett, Philip Pullman and Zadie Smith were among those who campaigned to save it.

BSP-KNR.name: Islamia Primary School
BSP-KNR.text: Your train passes near Islamia Primary School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1983 by the singer Yusuf Islam, known before as Cat Stevens. In 1998 it became the first Muslim school in Britain to be granted public funding, after a campaign of 13 years.

BSP-BSY.name: Kiln Theatre
BSP-BSY.text: Your train passes near the Kiln Theatre, on the train's {side}, opened on Kilburn High Road in 1980 as the Tricycle and renamed in 2018. It became known for plays made from the words spoken at public inquiries, as well as new writing.

BSY-WHD.name: Decca Studios
BSY-WHD.text: Your train passes near the former Decca Studios, on the train's {side}, at 165 Broadhurst Gardens, where Decca made its recordings from 1937. David Bowie recorded his first single there in 1964, and the Zombies their hit 'She's Not There'.

FNY-WHD.name: JW3
FNY-WHD.text: Your train passes near JW3, on the train's {side}, the Jewish Community Centre London, opened on Finchley Road in 2013. Its name plays on its postcode, NW3, and the idea came from Vivien Duffield's visit to a Jewish community centre in Manhattan in 2003.

FNY-HDH.name: Keats House
FNY-HDH.text: Your train passes near Keats House, on the train's {side}, where the poet John Keats lodged from 1818 to 1820. According to his friend Charles Brown, 'Ode to a Nightingale' was written under a plum tree in the garden, and here Keats fell in love with Fanny Brawne, who lived next door.

GPO-HDH.name: Parliament Hill Lido
GPO-HDH.text: Your train passes near Parliament Hill Lido, on the train's {side}, an open-air pool first opened in 1938. It is unheated and open all year, though from September to April only for early-morning swims.

GPO-KTW.name: Camden Town Brewery
GPO-KTW.text: Your train passes over Camden Town Brewery, which began brewing in 2010 in five Victorian railway arches beneath Kentish Town West station. Its founder, Jasper Cuppaidge, first brewed at The Horseshoe, his pub in Hampstead, using one of his grandfather's recipes.

GPO-UHL.name: Little Green Street
GPO-UHL.text: Your train passes Little Green Street, on the train's {side}, a tiny Kentish Town street of houses built in the 1780s, eight on one side and two on the other. It is one of the few intact Georgian streets left in London, and its houses are listed at Grade II.

CRH-UHL.name: Whittington Park
CRH-UHL.text: Your train passes near Whittington Park, on the train's {side}, named, like the nearby Whittington Hospital, after Dick Whittington. A large topiary cat, after his legendary pet, stands at the Holloway Road entrance.

CRH-HRY.name: Harringay Arena
CRH-HRY.text: Your train passes near the site of Harringay Arena, on the train's {side}, an eight-sided arena put up in eight months in 1936. It held the basketball and wrestling of the 1948 Olympics and Billy Graham's first crusade in Britain in 1954, and closed in 1958.

CRH-HGY.name: Railway Fields
CRH-HGY.text: Your train passes near Railway Fields, on the train's {side}, a railway goods yard until 1967 and now a nature reserve of about one hectare. More than 200 kinds of wild flower have been recorded there, among them the Haringey knotweed, a hybrid first found in 1987.

HGY-HRN.name: Konk
HGY-HRN.text: Your train passes near Konk, on the train's {side}, the recording studio the Kinks set up in Hornsey in the early 1970s, a mile from their home ground of Muswell Hill. Ray and Dave Davies paid for it partly with money from hits such as 'Lola', and the band recorded there full-time from about 1973.

AAP-HRN.name: St Mary's Tower, Hornsey
AAP-HRN.text: Your train passes near St Mary's Tower, on the train's {side}, all that is left of Hornsey's medieval parish church and the oldest building in Hornsey. Its date isn't known; the antiquarian Daniel Lysons seems to have been the first to put it at about 1500.

AAP-NSG.name: Bluebell Wood
AAP-NSG.text: Your train passes near Bluebell Wood, on the train's {side}, just over an acre of oak wood that is the last fragment of Tottenham Wood, which covered about 388 acres in 1619. Despite its name, no native bluebells grow there.

NSG-OKL.name: Friern Hospital
NSG-OKL.text: Your train passes near the former Friern Hospital, on the train's {side}, opened in 1851 as Colney Hatch Lunatic Asylum. At its height it held 2,500 patients and had the longest corridor in Britain; it closed in 1993 and became housing.

NBA-OKL.name: New Barnet War Memorial
NBA-OKL.text: Your train passes near New Barnet War Memorial, on the train's {side}, built in 1921 with a bronze figure of winged victory on top. It names 277 men and one woman of the district who died in the First World War; 136 names from the Second World War were added later.

HDW-NBA.name: Monken Hadley Common
HDW-NBA.text: Your train passes near Monken Hadley Common, on the train's {side}, a wedge of common land between Monken Hadley and Cockfosters. It is a remnant of the royal forest of Enfield Chase, enclosed by an Act of Parliament in 1777.

AAP-BOP.name: Bounds Green tube station
AAP-BOP.text: Your train passes near Bounds Green tube station, on the train's {side}, opened in 1932 on the Piccadilly line's extension to Cockfosters. Its eight-sided entrance was designed by C. H. James in the style of Charles Holden, a well-preserved example of London Transport's modern look of the 1930s.

BOP-PAL.name: Broomfield House
BOP-PAL.text: Your train passes near Broomfield House, on the train's {side}, in Broomfield Park. Bought by the London merchant Joseph Jackson in 1624, it was damaged by fires in 1984, 1993, 1994 and 2019, and plans to restore it had made no progress by January 2024.

PAL-WIH.name: Intimate Theatre
PAL-WIH.text: Your train passes near the Intimate Theatre, on the train's {side}, the name long used for St Monica's church hall on Green Lanes. The actor John Clements made it a theatre in 1935; Roger Moore later acted in its repertory company, and David Bowie appeared on its stage in 1968.

GPK-WIH.name: Grange Park Methodist Church
GPK-WIH.text: Your train passes near Grange Park Methodist Church, on the train's {side}, also known as the Church in the Orchard. Designed by Charles H. Brightiff in the Art Deco style, it opened in 1938.

ENC-GPK.name: Trinity Church, Enfield
ENC-GPK.text: Your train passes near Trinity Church, Enfield, on the train's {side}, a ragstone church with a tall spire, built for the Methodists in 1889. Badly damaged by fire in 1919, it reopened the next year; in the Second World War its basement was an air raid precautions control centre.

ENC-GDH.name: St Michael and All Angels, Enfield
ENC-GDH.text: Your train passes near St Michael and All Angels church, on the train's {side}, begun in 1873. A year later the money ran out, and the unfinished west end was closed off with a temporary wall that was not replaced until 1963.

CWH-GDH.name: Lavender Hill Cemetery
CWH-GDH.text: Your train passes near Lavender Hill Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1872 with two facing Gothic chapels, one for Anglicans and one for nonconformists. Its gates were “Cemetery Gates”, the end of Stan and Jack's bus route in the sitcom On the Buses.

FPK-HGY.name: New Beacon Books
FPK-HGY.text: Your train passes near New Beacon Books, on the train's {side}, founded in 1966 by John La Rose and Sarah White as the first Caribbean publishing house in England. Its bookshop has been at 76 Stroud Green Road since 1973, with the George Padmore Institute on the floors above.

DYP-FPK.name: Emirates Stadium
DYP-FPK.text: Your train passes near the Emirates Stadium, on the train's {side}, Arsenal's home since 2006. The club built it on an industrial and waste site at Ashburton Grove after being refused permission to enlarge Highbury; it seats more than 60,000.

DYP-HHY.name: Islington Central Library
DYP-HHY.text: Your train passes near Islington Central Library, on the train's {side}, opened in 1907 as the largest municipal library in London, partly paid for by Andrew Carnegie. Its architect, Henry T. Hare, was known for putting a hare somewhere in his designs.

CIR-HHY.name: HM Prison Pentonville
CIR-HHY.text: Your train passes near HM Prison Pentonville, on the train's {side}, opened in 1842 with four wings radiating from a central hall, so that staff could see along them all. It became the model for British prisons: 54 more were built to similar designs within six years.

CNN-HHY.name: Canonbury Tower
CNN-HHY.text: Your train passes near Canonbury Tower, on the train's {side}, the oldest building in Islington: the main surviving part of a manor house built for the canons of St Bartholomew's Priory between 1509 and 1532. Thomas Cromwell, Francis Bacon and Oliver Goldsmith were among its owners or occupants.

EXR-HHY.name: Union Chapel
EXR-HHY.text: Your train passes near Union Chapel, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed Gothic Revival church of the late 19th century that is still a working Congregational church. It is also a music venue known for its acoustics, and a drop-in centre for people facing homelessness.

EXR-OLD.name: Bunhill Fields
EXR-OLD.text: Your train passes near Bunhill Fields, on the train's {side}, a burial ground from 1665 to 1854 that took about 123,000 burials. John Bunyan, Daniel Defoe and William Blake are among those buried there; most of it is now a public garden.

MOG-OLD.name: John Wesley's House
MOG-OLD.text: Your train passes near John Wesley's House, on the train's {side}, built in 1779 beside Wesley's Chapel on City Road. John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, lived there for the last 12 years of his life and died in his bedroom.

MOG-ZFD.name: London Charterhouse
MOG-ZFD.text: Your train passes near the London Charterhouse, on the train's {side}, founded as a Carthusian priory in 1371 on the site of a Black Death burial ground. Thomas Sutton bought it in 1611 for a school and an almshouse; the almshouse is still lived in, while the school moved to Godalming in 1872.

TCR-ZFD.name: Sir John Soane's Museum
TCR-ZFD.text: Your train passes near Sir John Soane's Museum, on the train's {side}, the architect's own house, full of his drawings, models, paintings and antiquities. An Act of Parliament of 1833 left it to the nation, to be kept as nearly as possible as he left it, partly so that he could disinherit a son he disliked.

BDS-TCR.name: 25 Brook Street
BDS-TCR.text: Your train passes near 25 Brook Street, on the train's {side}, where the composer George Frideric Handel lived from 1723 until his death in 1759 and wrote almost all his later works. Jimi Hendrix lived next door at number 23; the two houses are now the museum Handel Hendrix House.

BDS-PAD.name: Marble Arch
BDS-PAD.text: Your train passes near Marble Arch, on the train's {side}, designed by John Nash in 1827 as the state entrance to the courtyard of Buckingham Palace. It was moved here, near the corner of Hyde Park, in 1851, when Queen Victoria enlarged the palace.

MOG-ZLW.name: Christ Church Spitalfields
MOG-ZLW.text: Your train passes near Christ Church Spitalfields, on the train's {side}, built between 1714 and 1729 to Nicholas Hawksmoor's design. It was one of the first churches of the commission set up in 1711 to build 50 new churches for London's new districts.

SDC-ZLW.name: The Theatre
SDC-ZLW.text: Your train passes near the site of The Theatre, on the train's {side}, built by James Burbage in 1576 as the first permanent theatre in England made only for plays. Shakespeare's company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men, played there; after a dispute with the landlord its timbers went to build the Globe on Bankside.

HOX-SDC.name: Museum of the Home
HOX-SDC.text: Your train passes near the Museum of the Home, on the train's {side}, formerly the Geffrye Museum, in almshouses built in 1714 for the widows of ironmongers with money left by Sir Robert Geffrye, a Lord Mayor of London. It explores home life from 1600 to the present day.

HGG-HOX.name: Hoxton Hall
HGG-HOX.text: Your train passes near Hoxton Hall, on the train's {side}, built as MacDonald's Music Hall in 1863. It lost its licence in 1871 after complaints by the police, and was later a Quaker meeting house for many years, which is why its galleried auditorium survives largely as it was built.

DLJ-HGG.name: Clowns Gallery and Archives
DLJ-HGG.text: Your train passes near the Clowns Gallery and Archives, on the train's {side}, set up in 1959 in the vestry of Holy Trinity Church, Dalston, and closed since 2018. It keeps the Clown Egg Register: since 1946, clowns' face designs have been painted on eggs so that no two clowns share a face.

DLJ-DLK.name: Vortex Jazz Club
DLJ-DLK.text: Your train passes near the Vortex Jazz Club, on the train's {side}, founded by David Mossman in 1988 in Stoke Newington Church Street. It moved to Gillett Square in Dalston in 2005, and the square opened the next year with a performance by 200 saxophonists.

DLK-SFA.name: St Augustine's Tower
DLK-SFA.text: Your train passes near St Augustine's Tower, on the train's {side}, all that is left of Hackney's early 16th-century parish church. A working 16th-century turret clock has been inside since at least 1608, and the tower appears on the London Borough of Hackney's coat of arms.

DLK-HKC.name: Rio Cinema
DLK-HKC.text: Your train passes near the Rio Cinema, on the train's {side}, which opened as the Kingsland Palace in 1909 and was rebuilt as the Kingsland Empire in 1915. F. E. Bromige gave it its Art Deco look in 1937; it was renamed the Rio in 1976, and from 1979 local people ran it as a community cooperative.

HKC-HMN.name: Sutton House
HKC-HMN.text: Your train passes near Sutton House, on the train's {side}, built in 1535 by Sir Ralph Sadler, Henry VIII's Principal Secretary of State. The oldest home in Hackney, it is a rare red-brick Tudor house and belongs to the National Trust.

HMN-SFA.name: V&A East
HMN-SFA.text: Your train passes near V&A East, on the train's {side}, the Victoria and Albert Museum's outpost in the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park. Its storehouse opened in May 2025 and its museum on April 18th 2026, the V&A's sixth site.

HKW-HMN.name: St Mary of Eton
HKW-HMN.text: Your train passes near St Mary of Eton church, on the train's {side}, built in 1890 to 1892 for a mission that Eton College set up in Hackney Wick, to help local people and show its pupils how they lived. The 59 Club, a Church of England youth club, was founded there.

HKW-SRA.name: London Aquatics Centre
HKW-SRA.text: Your train passes near the London Aquatics Centre, on the train's {side}, designed by Zaha Hadid for the swimming and diving at the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Under its wave-like roof are two swimming pools and a diving pool; it opened to the public in 2014.

BET-SRA.name: ArcelorMittal Orbit
BET-SRA.text: Your train passes near the ArcelorMittal Orbit, on the train's {side}, a 114.5-metre sculpture and observation tower by Anish Kapoor and Cecil Balmond, built for the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. It is Britain's largest piece of public art; in 2016 a slide, then the world's longest, was added.

BET-LST.name: All Hallows-on-the-Wall
BET-LST.text: Your train passes near All Hallows-on-the-Wall, on the train's {side}, a church beside the line of London's old city wall. The present building was designed by George Dance the Younger in 1767, when he was only 24; the church before it was known for the hermits who lived in cells there.

BET-CBH.name: Young V&A
BET-CBH.text: Your train passes near the Young V&A, on the train's {side}, the V&A's museum for children, opened in 1872 as the Bethnal Green Museum. Its iron frame was first put up in South Kensington in 1856 to 1857; the museum won Museum of the Year in 2024.

CBH-LOF.name: Keeling House
CBH-LOF.text: Your train passes near Keeling House, on the train's {side}, a 16-storey block designed by Denys Lasdun and finished in 1957. He grouped four blocks of maisonettes round a central tower, hoping to keep the neighbourliness of Victorian terraced streets; it was renovated in 2001 with a new penthouse floor.

HAC-LOF.name: Hackney Empire
HAC-LOF.text: Your train passes near the Hackney Empire, on the train's {side}, designed by Frank Matcham and built in 1901 as a music hall. Charlie Chaplin, Stan Laurel, Marie Lloyd and Gracie Fields all performed there.

HAC-REC.name: Mossbourne Community Academy
HAC-REC.text: Your train passes near Mossbourne Community Academy, on the train's {side}, opened in 2004 on the site of Hackney Downs School. Sir Clive Bourne founded it as one of England's first city academies, and its buildings were designed by Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners.

REC-SKW.name: Gibson Gardens
REC-SKW.text: Your train passes near Gibson Gardens, on the train's {side}, tenement flats built in 1880 by the Metropolitan Association for Improving the Dwellings of the Industrious Classes. They were some of the first good-quality homes in London for working and lower-middle-class families.

SKW-SMH.name: Abney Park Cemetery
SKW-SMH.text: Your train passes near Abney Park Cemetery, on the train's {side}, one of London's “Magnificent Seven” cemeteries, opened in 1840 as a non-denominational garden cemetery and arboretum. Nearly 197,000 burials had taken place there by 2000; it is now a local nature reserve.

SMH-SVS.name: St Ignatius Church, Stamford Hill
SMH-SVS.text: Your train passes near St Ignatius Church, on the train's {side}, a large Roman Catholic church run by the Jesuits. Cardinal Herbert Vaughan invited them to found the parish, which they did in 1894, after nearly 300 local people had asked for one.

BCV-SVS.name: Marcus Garvey Library
BCV-SVS.text: Your train passes near the Marcus Garvey Library, on the train's {side}, opened in 1987 and named after the activist Marcus Garvey, whose son, Marcus Garvey III, laid its foundation stone. Its Black Literature and Marcus Garvey collections are used by the local Black community.

BCV-WHL.name: Bruce Castle
BCV-WHL.text: Your train passes near Bruce Castle, on the train's {side}, a 16th-century manor house and one of the oldest surviving English brick houses. The postal reformer Sir Rowland Hill lived there; it is now a museum, and its grounds, a park since 1892, are Tottenham's oldest.

SLV-WHL.name: Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
SLV-WHL.text: Your train passes near Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, on the train's {side}, opened on April 3rd 2019 on the site of the club's old ground, White Hart Lane, and land beside it. With 62,850 seats it is the largest club ground in London, and its pitch slides away to reveal an artificial one for American football.

EDR-SLV.name: Pymmes Park
EDR-SLV.text: Your train passes near Pymmes Park, on the train's {side}, named after Pymmes House, built there by William Pymme in 1327. William Cecil, Lord Burghley, bought the estate in 1582; the council bought it for a public park, which opened in 1906.

BHK-EDR.name: All Saints' Church, Edmonton
BHK-EDR.text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church, Edmonton, on the train's {side}, first recorded in the 12th century and rebuilt in the 15th; its west tower still has its medieval outside. The essayist Charles Lamb and his sister Mary, a writer, are buried there.

BHK-ENF.name: Barclays Bank, Enfield
BHK-ENF.text: Your train passes near Barclays Bank in Enfield, on the train's {side}, where the world's first cash machine was put in, in 1967. A gold-coloured cash machine and a plaque have marked the spot since 2017; the building itself was finished in 1897.

EDR-SBU.name: Ripaults Factory
EDR-SBU.text: Your train passes near the Ripaults Factory, on the train's {side}, a listed art deco building designed by A. H. Durnford for a firm that made electrical cables and parts for motor vehicles. Built in the 1930s, it has since been used by the lorry maker MAN and then a builders' merchant.

SBU-TUR.name: St James' Church, Enfield Highway
SBU-TUR.text: Your train passes near St James' Church, Enfield Highway, on the train's {side}, consecrated on October 15th 1831. Built by subscription as a chapel of ease, it was the first Anglican church in the parish of Enfield besides the parish church itself.

CPT-HAC.name: Clapton Cinematograph Theatre
CPT-HAC.text: Your train passes near the Clapton Cinematograph Theatre, on the train's {side}, opened on December 16th 1910 and one of the earliest purpose-built cinemas in London. It was built after new safety rules of 1909, as film then was highly flammable, and seated 750.

CPT-TOM.name: Walthamstow Marshes
CPT-TOM.text: Your train passes Walthamstow Marshes, on the train's {side}, one of the last pieces of near-natural wetland in Greater London. In 1909 Alliott Verdon Roe made the first all-British powered flight across them, in his Roe I Triplane; he went on to found Avro.

LEB-TOM.name: Markfield Beam Engine
LEB-TOM.text: Your train passes near the Markfield Beam Engine, on the train's {side}, built in 1886 to pump Tottenham's sewage towards Beckton. Its flywheel is 27 feet across, and it is the only Wood Brothers eight-column engine still where it was installed.

NUM-TOM.name: Tottenham Marshes
NUM-TOM.text: Your train passes near Tottenham Marshes, on the train's {side}, part of the Lee Valley Park since 1972. Tottenham Hotspur played their first matches there, in 1882, before moving to an enclosed ground.

MRW-NUM.name: Glover and Main
MRW-NUM.text: Your train passes near the site of Glover and Main's Gothic Works, on the train's {side}, where gas meters were made from 1897. Thomas Glover had invented the diaphragm gas meter in 1843, and the firm became one of Britain's biggest makers of gas cookers.

MRW-PON.name: Wright's Flour Mill
MRW-PON.text: Your train passes near Wright's Flour Mill, on the train's {side}, Enfield's oldest working industrial building, with parts dating from 1789. There has been a mill there since at least the late 16th century; the Wright family still own it.

BMD-PON.name: Beavertown Brewery
BMD-PON.text: Your train passes near Beavertown Brewery, on the train's {side}, founded in 2011 by Logan Plant, son of Led Zeppelin's Robert Plant. Its name comes from De Beauvoir Town, where its first beer was brewed; its Enfield brewery opened in 2020.

BMD-ENL.name: Enfield Power Station
BMD-ENL.text: Your train passes near Enfield Power Station, on the train's {side}, a 442-megawatt gas-fired station on part of the site of the old Brimsdown Power Station. Building started in September 1997, and it was running by December 1999.

ENL-WLC.name: The Eleanor Cross, Waltham Cross
ENL-WLC.text: Your train passes near the Eleanor Cross at Waltham Cross, on the train's {side}, one of only three of Edward I's crosses for his queen, Eleanor of Castile, still standing. They marked where her coffin rested on its way from Lincoln to Westminster Abbey in 1290; the town is named after it.

LEB-SRA.name: Lee Valley VeloPark
LEB-SRA.text: Your train passes near the Lee Valley VeloPark, on the train's {side}, with its velodrome built for the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. It also has a BMX track, a one-mile road course and five miles of mountain bike trails, and opened to the public in March 2014.

SRA-ZLW.name: St Dunstan's, Stepney
SRA-ZLW.text: Your train passes near St Dunstan's, Stepney, on the train's {side}, believed to have been founded or refounded by St Dunstan in about 952. It is known as the Mother Church of the East End, and as the Church of the High Seas.

SDE-ZLW.name: Trinity Green Almshouses
SDE-ZLW.text: Your train passes near Trinity Green Almshouses, on the train's {side}, built by Trinity House in 1695 for retired sailors and their widows. Saved from demolition in the 1890s by a public campaign, they were the first buildings on the register that grew into today's listed buildings.

CWX-ZLW.name: St Anne's Limehouse
CWX-ZLW.text: Your train passes near St Anne's Limehouse, on the train's {side}, designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor and consecrated in 1730. Being so close to the river, it was given the right to fly the White Ensign of the Royal Navy.

CUS-CWX.name: Billingsgate Fish Market
CUS-CWX.text: Your train passes near Billingsgate Fish Market, on the train's {side}, the largest inland fish market in the United Kingdom. It moved here, by the West India Docks, from the City of London in 1982; in the 19th century, Billingsgate was the largest fish market in the world.

CUS-WWC.name: Woolwich Ferry
CUS-WWC.text: Your train passes near the Woolwich Ferry, on the train's {side}, a free vehicle and foot ferry across the Thames. A ferry has run at Woolwich since the 14th century; the free service began in 1889, and about two million passengers use it each year.

ABW-WWC.name: The Royal Arsenal's Grand Store
ABW-WWC.text: Your train passes near the Royal Arsenal's Grand Store, on the train's {side}, a great three-sided range of riverside warehouses built in 1805 to 1813 to James Wyatt's design. Wooden piles were used instead of the stone foundations he specified, and the buildings suffered from subsidence for many years.

ABW-PLU.name: St Nicholas Church, Plumstead
ABW-PLU.text: Your train passes near St Nicholas Church, Plumstead, on the train's {side}, on a site with a church since about the 10th century. Its oldest part, now the south aisle, is 12th and 13th century, and its tower dates from 1664; it was badly damaged by flying bombs in 1944 and 1945.

PLU-WWA.name: The site of the Manor Ground
PLU-WWA.text: Your train passes near the site of the Manor Ground, on the train's {side}, home from 1888 of Royal Arsenal, the club that became Arsenal. The pitch was famously muddy, and with no stands, wagons borrowed from army bases nearby held the crowds.

WWA-WWD.name: The Royal Brass Foundry
WWA-WWD.text: Your train passes near the Royal Brass Foundry, on the train's {side}, built for the Board of Ordnance's own gun foundry, set up in 1717. It is tall inside, for a machine that bored cannon upright, and has tall doors to get the new guns out; the foundry was renamed the Royal Gun Factory in 1855.

CTN-WWD.name: The Valley
CTN-WWD.text: Your train passes near The Valley, on the train's {side}, home of Charlton Athletic since 1919. Supporters dug out the pitch themselves in an old sand and chalk pit; it now holds 27,111.

BKH-CTN.name: Morden College
BKH-CTN.text: Your train passes near Morden College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1695 by Sir John Morden as a home for merchants who had fallen on hard times. Its design is sometimes said to be by Sir Christopher Wren; it is still a retirement home, and its day centre won the Stirling Prize in 2023.

BKH-LEW.name: Blackheath Quaker Meeting House
BKH-LEW.text: Your train passes near Blackheath Quaker Meeting House, on the train's {side}, designed by Trevor Dannatt and used by Quakers since 1972. It is thought to be the only Quaker meeting house in Britain built in the Brutalist style, and has been called a “Brutalist jewel”.

LEW-NHD.name: Telegraph Hill
LEW-NHD.text: Your train passes near Telegraph Hill, on the train's {side}, once called Plowed Garlic Hill. It takes its name from a semaphore telegraph station built on top in about 1795, one of the points from which news of Wellington's victory at Waterloo was passed to London.

NHD-PMR.name: Nunhead Cemetery
NHD-PMR.text: Your train passes near Nunhead Cemetery, on the train's {side}, consecrated in 1840 as All Saints' Cemetery. One of two of London's “Magnificent Seven” Victorian cemeteries south of the Thames, it is now a local nature reserve.

DMK-PMR.name: Maudsley Hospital
DMK-PMR.text: Your train passes near the Maudsley Hospital, on the train's {side}, the largest mental health training institution in the UK. The psychiatrist Henry Maudsley offered £30,000 in 1907 towards a hospital for early and acute cases, with teaching and research.

EDW-PMR.name: House of Dreams
EDW-PMR.text: Your train passes near the House of Dreams, on the train's {side}, an ordinary terraced house that the designer Stephen Wright has turned into his own art museum since 1998. It is a memorial to his late partner and his parents, and opens to visitors about ten times a year.

EDW-NDL.name: James Allen's Girls' School
EDW-NDL.text: Your train passes near James Allen's Girls' School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1741 and the second-oldest independent girls' school in Great Britain. It began as part of Edward Alleyn's charity, with Dulwich College and Alleyn's School.

NDL-TUH.name: Herne Hill Velodrome
NDL-TUH.text: Your train passes near Herne Hill Velodrome, on the train's {side}, built in 1891 and one of the oldest cycle tracks in the world. It hosted the track cycling at the 1948 Olympics, and Crystal Palace football club played there during the First World War.

STE-TUH.name: Streatham Ice and Leisure Centre
STE-TUH.text: Your train passes near Streatham Ice and Leisure Centre, on the train's {side}, London's only Olympic-sized ice rink and home of the Streatham ice hockey teams. It replaced Streatham Ice Arena, opened on the site on February 26th 1931.

STE-TOO.name: St Barnabas' Church, Mitcham
STE-TOO.text: Your train passes near St Barnabas' Church, Mitcham, on the train's {side}, designed by H. P. Burke Downing and finished on November 14th 1914. It replaced a simple one-room “tin church” used by the mission set up there in 1906.

HYR-TOO.name: Wandle Meadow Nature Park
HYR-TOO.text: Your train passes near Wandle Meadow Nature Park, on the train's {side}, beside the River Wandle. Part of a sewage works from 1877 to 1970, it was proposed as a site for a Wimbledon football stadium, but local people opposed it and it became a nature reserve in 1989.

HYR-WIM.name: The site of Plough Lane
HYR-WIM.text: Your train passes near the site of Plough Lane, on the train's {side}, Wimbledon Football Club's ground from September 1912 until 1991. It was demolished in 2002, and the houses built there are named Reynolds Gate after the Wimbledon striker Eddie Reynolds.

BAL-TOO.name: The Bedford, Balham
BAL-TOO.text: Your train passes near The Bedford in Balham, on the train's {side}, a listed pub rebuilt in about 1931 and known for comedy and music. The Clash, U2 and Ed Sheeran have all played early gigs there.

BAL-MTC.name: Battersea Grammar School
BAL-MTC.text: Your train passes near the site of Battersea Grammar School, on the train's {side}. Founded in Battersea in 1875, the school moved to larger premises in Streatham in 1936, and closed in 1977 when it merged with Rosa Bassett School, a girls' grammar school, to form Furzedown Secondary School in Tooting.

MIJ-MTC.name: Mitcham Cricket Green
MIJ-MTC.text: Your train passes near Mitcham Cricket Green, on the train's {side}, where cricket has been played since 1685. Touring Australian teams of the 19th century stayed at the Cricketers pub, which overlooked the green, and practised on the green, and its pavilion, built in 1904, is one of the few cut off from their ground by a road.

HCB-MIJ.name: BedZED
HCB-MIJ.text: Your train passes near BedZED, the Beddington Zero Energy Development, on the train's {side}. Designed by the architect Bill Dunster and built from 2000 to 2002, its 82 homes made up the first large community designed to give off no carbon emissions, and it was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize in 2003.

CSH-HCB.name: Wilderness Island
CSH-HCB.text: Your train passes near Wilderness Island, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of almost three hectares on the island between the rivers Wandle and Wrythe in Carshalton. A fish pond survives from a public garden that was once here, and kingfishers and the rare hornet clearwing moth can be found.

MTC-STE.name: Oakleigh Way
MTC-STE.text: Your train passes Oakleigh Way, on the train's {side}, a local nature reserve of less than a hectare in Mitcham. It was once a railway depot and sidings, and is now birch woodland with scrub and grassland, where weld and zigzag clover grow.

SRC-STE.name: St Leonard's Church, Streatham
