SRC-STE.text: Your train passes near St Leonard's Church, Streatham, on the train's {side}, the parish church of a parish named in the Domesday Book. The lower part of its tower dates from the 14th century; almost all the rest was rebuilt in 1830 and 1831, and the church was restored after a fire gutted it on May 5th 1975.

BAL-SRH.name: Du Cane Court
BAL-SRH.text: Your train passes near Du Cane Court, on the train's {side}, an Art Deco block of 677 flats on Balham High Road. When it was built in 1937 it was thought to be the largest privately owned block of flats in Europe, and many music hall stars of the 1930s and 1940s lived there, among them the comedian Tommy Trinder.

TUH-WNW.name: St Luke's Church, West Norwood
TUH-WNW.text: Your train passes near St Luke's Church, West Norwood, on the train's {side}, one of four "Waterloo churches" named after the four Gospel writers. Designed by Francis Octavius Bedford as a result of the Church Building Act of 1818, it was consecrated on July 25th 1825, on a triangular site where Norwood Road forks.

HNH-TUH.name: South London Botanical Institute
HNH-TUH.text: Your train passes near the South London Botanical Institute, on the train's {side}, founded in 1910 by Allan Octavian Hume in a large Victorian house on Norwood Road. It has changed little since, keeping its library, a herbarium of pressed plants and a small botanic garden with more than 500 species.

HNH-WDU.name: Half Moon, Herne Hill
HNH-WDU.text: Your train passes the Half Moon, on the train's {side}, a corner pub of 1896 that is one of only 270 pubs on CAMRA's National Inventory of Historic Pub Interiors. The poet Dylan Thomas drank there, and for nearly 50 years it was a live music venue: U2 played there three times in 1980.

SYH-WDU.name: Dulwich College
SYH-WDU.text: Your train passes near Dulwich College, on the train's {side}, founded on June 21st 1619 by the Elizabethan actor Edward Alleyn as the College of God's Gift, to educate 12 poor scholars. It grew into a large school from 1857, and moved into its present buildings in 1870.

PNE-SYH.name: Six Pillars
PNE-SYH.text: Your train passes near Six Pillars, on the train's {side}, a modernist house built from 1932 to 1934 for John Leakey, headmaster of Dulwich College Preparatory School. Its architect, Valentine Harding of the Tecton group, based it on Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye, but used London stock brick so it wouldn't stand out among its Victorian neighbours.

KTH-PNE.name: Royal Watermen's Almshouses
KTH-PNE.text: Your train passes near the Royal Watermen's Almshouses, on the train's {side}, built in 1840 and 1841 by the Company of Watermen and Lightermen of the City of London for retired freemen and their widows. They are the oldest Victorian almshouses in Penge; the residents moved to Hastings in 1973, and the buildings became private homes.

BKJ-KTH.name: St George's Church, Beckenham
BKJ-KTH.text: Your train passes near St George's Church, Beckenham, on the train's {side}. First built in the 12th century, it was rebuilt from 1885 to 1887 by the local architect W. Gibbs Bartleet, and its pinnacled tower, finished in 1903, is the focal point of Beckenham High Street.

BIK-BKJ.name: Beckenham Cemetery
BIK-BKJ.text: Your train passes near Beckenham Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1876 as the Crystal Palace District Cemetery. The cricketer W. G. Grace and the businessman Thomas Crapper are buried there.

BIK-CYP.name: National Sports Centre, Crystal Palace
BIK-CYP.text: Your train passes near the National Sports Centre, on the train's {side}, opened in Crystal Palace Park in 1964. It stands on the site of the ground where FA Cup finals were played from 1895 to 1914, and its athletics stadium has also staged concerts by Bruce Springsteen and the Sex Pistols.

CYP-GIP.name: Crystal Palace transmitting station
CYP-GIP.text: Your train passes near the Crystal Palace transmitting station, on the train's {side}, the main television transmitter for London, on the site of a television station run by John Logie Baird from 1933. Standing on a hill 109 metres high, it is the highest structure above sea level in London.

GIP-WNW.name: West Norwood Cemetery
GIP-WNW.text: Your train passes near West Norwood Cemetery, on the train's {side}, consecrated on December 7th 1837 and one of London's "Magnificent Seven" Victorian cemeteries. Its 69 listed monuments and buildings include a Greek Orthodox burial ground with 19 listed mausoleums and monuments.

CYP-NWD.name: St John the Evangelist, Upper Norwood
CYP-NWD.text: Your train passes near the Church of St John the Evangelist, Upper Norwood, on the train's {side}, a red-brick Gothic Revival church built from 1878 to 1887 to the designs of John Loughborough Pearson. It replaced a large iron church moved to the site in 1875 to serve the new suburb.

NWD-SRS.name: Holy Innocents Church, South Norwood
NWD-SRS.text: Your train passes near Holy Innocents Church, South Norwood, on the train's {side}, built in 1894 and 1895 to the designs of George Frederick Bodley, in imitation of the late Gothic Perpendicular style. The tower he planned for it was never built.

ECR-SRS.name: No. 1 Croydon
ECR-SRS.text: Your train passes near the "50p Building", on the train's {side}, the 24-storey tower next to East Croydon station that was first called the NLA Tower and is also known as the "Threepenny Bit". Designed by Richard Seifert and Partners and finished in 1970, it gets its distinctive look from floors with cut-off corners, set one above another at alternating angles.

ECR-SCY.name: Fairfield Halls
ECR-SCY.text: Your train passes near Fairfield Halls, on the train's {side}, an arts centre opened in 1962 with a large concert hall often used for BBC recordings. It stands on Croydon's old "Fair Field", home to a well-known fair until about 1860, above disused railway cuttings that once led from the line to Brighton to Croydon Central station.

PUO-SCY.name: Whitgift School
PUO-SCY.text: Your train passes near Whitgift School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1596 by John Whitgift, Archbishop of Canterbury, and opened in 1600. It moved here in 1931 to Haling Park, once the home of Lord Howard of Effingham, who commanded the English fleet against the Spanish Armada.

PUO-PUR.name: Purley War Memorial Hospital
PUO-PUR.text: Your train passes near Purley War Memorial Hospital, on the train's {side}. It began as a cottage hospital with eight beds, opened by Princess Helena, and after the First World War it reopened in 1922 as the district's war memorial hospital, with 22 beds.

PUR-RHM.name: Purley Council Offices
PUR-RHM.text: Your train passes near the former Purley Council Offices, on the train's {side}, a red-brick Neo-Georgian building that cost £30,000. The Lord Mayor of London opened it on November 8th 1930 as the headquarters of the Coulsdon and Purley Urban District Council.

CDN-RHM.name: Coulsdon North station
CDN-RHM.text: Your train passes the site of Coulsdon North station, on the train's {side}. It opened on November 5th 1899 as "Stoats Nest and Cane Hill", changed its name three times, and closed on October 3rd 1983 when the line to Brighton was resignalled.

CDN-WME.name: Coulsdon Town station
CDN-WME.text: Coulsdon Town station opened as Smitham on January 1st 1904 and kept that name until May 22nd 2011. It sits on a sharp curve, where the line to Tattenham Corner swings away westwards from the main line to Brighton.

CDN-CDS.name: Croydon, Merstham and Godstone Railway embankment
CDN-CDS.text: Your train passes near an embankment of the Croydon, Merstham and Godstone Railway, on the train's {side}. Opened in 1805 as an extension of the horse-drawn Surrey Iron Railway, the line ran to quarries near Merstham until 1838; this embankment at Coulsdon is eight metres high.

KLY-PUR.name: Foxley Wood
KLY-PUR.text: Your train passes near Foxley Wood, on the train's {side}, a local nature reserve of more than 11 hectares, partly ancient woodland of oak and ash, with patches of chalk grassland. The local council bought it in the 1930s to keep it as Green Belt, and badgers and roe deer live there.

KLY-WHY.name: Whyteleafe
KLY-WHY.text: Your train passes near Whyteleafe, on the train's {side}, a village in a dry valley of the North Downs with three railway stations on two lines. It takes its name from the whitebeam trees that grow here, whose leaves are white underneath.

SCY-SNR.name: Elmhurst School
SCY-SNR.text: Your train passes near Elmhurst School, on the train's {side}, a preparatory school that grew from two schools founded in 1869. One of them, run by the sisters Clarissa and Florence Prince, counted the young P. G. Wodehouse among its pupils in the 1880s, and moved into the house called Elmhurst in 1894.

RDD-SNR.name: Riddlesdown
RDD-SNR.text: Your train passes near Riddlesdown, on the train's {side}, a place recorded as Ridelesdowne in 1331; the "Riddle" part is thought to come from Middle English for "cleared woodland". Most of its houses were built in the 1930s by John Laing, some with an Art Deco touch, and Fred Perry opened its tennis club in June 1938.

RDD-UWL.name: Riddlesdown Common
RDD-UWL.text: Your train runs beside Riddlesdown Common, on the train's {side}, 43 hectares near the northern end of the North Downs, owned by the City of London Corporation, most of it a Site of Special Scientific Interest. Neolithic stone axes have been found there, and a trig point on top shows it is 525 feet above sea level.

ANZ-NWD.name: Anerley Town Hall
ANZ-NWD.text: Your train passes near Anerley Town Hall, on the train's {side}, an Italianate building by George Elkington, opened on April 30th 1879 as the vestry hall of St Paul's, Anerley. It became the headquarters of Penge Urban District in 1900; its assembly hall has an unusual hammerbeam roof tied with wrought-iron rods.

ANZ-PNW.name: Croydon Canal, Betts Park
ANZ-PNW.text: Your train is following the course of the Croydon Canal, which crossed Penge Common along what is now this line through Penge West; a stretch of it survives in Betts Park, on the train's {side}. After the canal closed, the London and Croydon Railway, at first an atmospheric railway, was built largely along its course and opened in 1839.

PNW-SYD.name: St Christopher's Hospice
PNW-SYD.text: Your train passes near St Christopher's Hospice, on the train's {side}, founded in 1967 by Cicely Saunders, whose work is the basis of the modern hospice movement. Its early staff began the first hospice home care, and one of them, Florence Wald, took the idea to the United States.

CYP-SYD.name: Crystal Palace Dinosaurs
CYP-SYD.text: Your train passes the Crystal Palace Dinosaurs, on the train's {side}, unveiled in 1854 as the first dinosaur sculptures in the world. Designed by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins with Sir Richard Owen, they show 15 kinds of extinct animal, only three of them true dinosaurs, and are listed Grade I.

FOH-SYD.name: Mayow Park
FOH-SYD.text: Your train passes near Mayow Park, on the train's {side}, opened in 1878 as Sydenham Recreation Ground on land owned by the Mayow family. It is the oldest park in the borough of Lewisham, and the tea merchant Frederick Horniman was on the committee formed to find the money and the land for it.

FOH-HPA.name: Horniman Museum
FOH-HPA.text: Your train passes near the Horniman Museum, on the train's {side}, opened in 1901 by the tea trader Frederick Horniman for his collection of some 30,000 objects. Designed by Charles Harrison Townsend, it is known for its natural history displays and musical instruments, and it was Museum of the Year in 2022.

BCY-HPA.name: Rivoli Ballroom
BCY-HPA.text: Your train passes near the Rivoli Ballroom, on the train's {side}, opened in July 1913 as the Crofton Park Picture Palace. After its last film in 1957 it became a dance hall, reopening on Boxing Day 1959 with a sprung floor of Canadian maple, and it keeps its red velvet, flock wallpaper and chandeliers.

BCY-NXG.name: New Cross Gate Cutting
BCY-NXG.text: Your train passes near New Cross Gate Cutting, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of more than four hectares beside the line. It is a remnant of the Great North Wood, on the site once known as Hatcham Wood, and deer live there; the London Wildlife Trust manages it and usually opens it only on open days.

LBG-NXG.name: St James's Church, Bermondsey
LBG-NXG.text: Your train passes near St James's Church, Bermondsey, on the train's {side}, designed by James Savage and consecrated in 1829, one of the churches paid for under the Church Building Acts. Its spire was inspired by Sir Christopher Wren's St Stephen Walbrook, and needed an Act of Parliament of its own in 1831 to borrow more money.

CST-LBG.name: Southwark Cathedral
CST-LBG.text: Your train passes near Southwark Cathedral, on the train's {side}, a place of Christian worship for more than a thousand years. It became a cathedral only when the Diocese of Southwark was created in 1905, and the building keeps the form of the Gothic church built between 1220 and 1420, though its nave was rebuilt in the late 19th century.

DEP-LBG.name: London Bridge to Greenwich Railway Viaduct
DEP-LBG.text: Your train runs along the viaduct of the London and Greenwich Railway, built between 1834 and 1836 and one of the oldest railway viaducts in the world. With 851 semi-circular arches and 27 skew arches or road bridges between London Bridge and Deptford Creek, it is the longest run of arches in Britain.

LBG-NWX.name: Maltby Street Market
LBG-NWX.text: Your train passes near Maltby Street Market, on the train's {side}, a weekly street-food and provisions market near Tower Bridge. The street was roughly the site of a ropewalk, in an area once known for making rigging and cable for sailing ships, and the market's yard is still called the Ropewalk.

LBG-SBM.name: Neckinger Mills
LBG-SBM.text: Your train passes near Neckinger Mills, on the train's {side}, a warehouse of the tanners Bevington & Sons, completed in 1864 and named after the River Neckinger, which now runs underground. A paper mill stood here before the firm took over the site in 1806.

QRP-SBM.name: The Den
QRP-SBM.text: Your train passes near The Den, on the train's {side}, home of Millwall Football Club since 1993, when it replaced the Old Den a quarter of a mile away. It is the sixth ground the club has had since it was formed on the Isle of Dogs in 1885.

PMR-QRP.name: Peckham Rye station
PMR-QRP.text: Peckham Rye station, at one end of this stretch, opened on December 1st 1865 and was designed by Charles Henry Driver, the architect of the Abbey Mills and Crossness pumping stations. Its platforms are on two separate viaducts, with a single ticket hall at ground level.

QRP-SQE.name: New Cross Stadium
QRP-SQE.text: Your train passes near the site of New Cross Stadium, on the train's {side}, opened on June 1st 1933 for greyhound racing and later used for speedway. Its tight, banked speedway track was known as "The Frying Pan". The stadium closed in 1969 and was demolished in 1975.

SQE-ZCW.name: Canada Water
SQE-ZCW.text: Your train passes near the lake of Canada Water, on the train's {side}, the surviving northern third of Canada Dock, which was mainly used by ships from Canada. After the docks closed in the 1970s, about half of the dock was filled in for the Surrey Quays Shopping Centre, and the rest became a lake and wildlife refuge.

ROE-ZCW.name: Brunel Museum
ROE-ZCW.text: Your train passes near the Brunel Museum, on the train's {side}, in the engine house Marc Brunel designed for the Thames Tunnel. The tunnel's shaft beside it was the world's first caisson: a brick tower 50 feet across, built above ground and then sunk under its own weight.

ROE-WPE.name: Thames Tunnel
ROE-WPE.text: Your train runs through the Thames Tunnel, the first tunnel known to have been built successfully under a navigable river. Marc Brunel and his son Isambard built it between 1825 and 1843 for horse-drawn carriages, but it was mostly used by people on foot until it became a railway tunnel in 1869.

SDE-WPE.name: St George in the East
SDE-WPE.text: Your train passes near St George in the East, on the train's {side}, one of the six churches Nicholas Hawksmoor designed in London, built from 1714 to 1729. Its walls and distinctive "pepper-pot" towers hold a modern church interior built inside them in 1964.

NXG-SQE.name: Sanford Housing Co-operative
NXG-SQE.text: Your train passes near Sanford Housing Co-operative, on the train's {side}, the first purpose-built housing co-operative in the United Kingdom, which has run without a break since it opened in 1974. About 120 people live there, in a street of shared houses and studio flats run by its members.

NWX-SQE.name: SELCHP
NWX-SQE.text: Your train passes near SELCHP, on the train's {side}, an energy-from-waste plant that can burn up to 420,000 tonnes of rubbish a year and generate up to 35 megawatts. It grew from Lewisham, Southwark and Greenwich councils coming together in 1986 to find an alternative to landfill.

NWX-SAJ.name: Stone House, Deptford
NWX-SAJ.text: Your train passes near Stone House, on the train's {side}, built between 1771 and 1773 by the architect George Gibson the younger for himself. Its design is so unusual that in the 19th century it was commonly known as the Comical House, and some maps of the time labelled it so.

LEW-SAJ.name: Brookmill Road Local Nature Reserve
LEW-SAJ.text: Your train passes near Brookmill Road Local Nature Reserve, on the train's {side}, on the embankment of a disused railway: its trains stopped in 1916 and the tracks were lifted in 1929. Lewisham Council bought the land in 1979 and made it a nature reserve, with three small ponds.

DEP-GNW.name: St Paul's, Deptford
DEP-GNW.text: Your train passes near St Paul's, Deptford, on the train's {side}, designed by Thomas Archer and built between 1712 and 1730. It is one of the 12 churches actually built of the 50 planned by the New Church Commissioners, and the Buildings of England calls it one of the most moving 18th-century churches in London.

GNW-MZH.name: National Maritime Museum
GNW-MZH.text: Your train passes near the National Maritime Museum, on the train's {side}, created by an Act of Parliament in 1934 and based largely on gifts from Sir James Caird. King George VI opened it on April 27th 1937.

MZH-WCB.name: East Greenwich Pleasaunce
MZH-WCB.text: Your train passes near East Greenwich Pleasaunce, on the train's {side}, a park that was once the graveyard of Greenwich Hospital. When a railway tunnel was built, the remains of about 3,000 sailors and officers, including men who had fought at Trafalgar, were moved here from the hospital's own grounds in 1875.

CTN-WCB.name: Woodlands House
CTN-WCB.text: Your train passes near Woodlands House, on the train's {side}, a Georgian villa built from 1774 to 1776 for John Julius Angerstein, whose art collection was bought in 1824 to form the core of the National Gallery. It was designed by the local architect George Gibson and now houses a Steiner school.

BKJ-NBC.name: Kent Championships
BKJ-NBC.text: Your train passes near Beckenham Cricket Club's ground in Foxgrove Road, on the train's {side}, where the Kent Championships, a grass-court tennis tournament, were played in the first half of June from 1886 to 1996.

CLK-NBC.name: HSBC Sports and Social Club
CLK-NBC.text: Your train passes near the HSBC Sports and Social Club ground, on the train's {side}, set up in 1920 and known as the Midland Bank Sports Ground until 1992. Kent played a single one-day match there, beating Lancashire in a rain-affected game in 1970, and the River Pool runs along its western edge.

CLK-ELE.name: Bowie Bandstand
CLK-ELE.text: Your train passes near the Bowie Bandstand, on the train's {side}, put up in 1905 in Croydon Road Recreation Ground and believed to be the only surviving bandstand by the McCallum and Hope Iron Foundry of Glasgow. On August 16th 1969 David Bowie helped organise, compere and perform at a free festival there.

EDN-ELE.name: Long Lane Wood
EDN-ELE.text: Your train passes near Long Lane Wood, on the train's {side}, 15 acres of ancient woodland, mostly English oak with the odd beech. It was part of the Great North Wood, and has a small fenced-off bird sanctuary at the back.

EDN-WWI.name: Wellcome Research Laboratories
EDN-WWI.text: Your train passes near the site of the Wellcome Research Laboratories, on the train's {side}. Henry Wellcome bought the 105-acre site in 1919 for £32,000, and its scientists developed the antibiotic trimethoprim; it closed in 1995, after Glaxo took Wellcome over.

HYS-WWI.name: St Mary the Virgin, Hayes
HYS-WWI.text: Your train passes near the church of St Mary the Virgin in Hayes, on the train's {side}, built in the 12th century and much enlarged in Victorian times to designs by Sir George Gilbert Scott and his son John Oldrid Scott.

LSY-NBC.name: County Cricket Ground, Beckenham
LSY-NBC.text: Your train passes near the County Ground, Beckenham, on the train's {side}, set up by Lloyds Bank in 1918 as its main sports ground near London. It was first used for first-class cricket in 1954, hosted two matches in the 1993 Women's Cricket World Cup, and has been a regular Kent outground since 2003.

CFB-LSY.name: Private Banks Sports Ground
CFB-LSY.text: Your train passes near the Private Banks Sports Ground, on the train's {side}, used by Kent for first-class cricket from 1875 to 1921. In 2012 it was sold to the educational foundation of nearby St Dunstan's College and renamed the Jubilee Ground.

CFB-LAD.name: Alex Yee Ladywell Arena
CFB-LAD.text: Your train passes near the Alex Yee Ladywell Arena, on the train's {side}, an athletics stadium renamed on November 22nd 2024 after the Olympic triathlete Alex Yee, who trained on its track early in his career. He asked for "Ladywell" to be kept in the name.

BKJ-SRT.name: Bishop Challoner School
BKJ-SRT.text: Your train passes near the former Bishop Challoner School, on the train's {side}, a Roman Catholic independent day school that began as a junior school and added a senior wing in 1956. It closed on July 4th 2025.

RVB-SRT.name: Bromley Reform Synagogue
RVB-SRT.text: Your train passes near Bromley Reform Synagogue, on the train's {side}, whose congregation was founded in 1964 and moved here in 1967. Its sanctuary was refurbished in light wood and glass to reflect the community's Hebrew name, Beit Or, House of Light.

BEC-RVB.name: Beckenham Place Park
BEC-RVB.text: Your train passes near Beckenham Place Park, on the train's {side}, a large park laid out by John Cator the younger in the second half of the 18th century. Its Palladian mansion, which gave the park its name, is now a community centre and café.

BEC-BGM.name: Catford Studios
BEC-BGM.text: Your train passes near the site of Catford Studios, on the train's {side}, a film studio built in 1914. During the First World War it made Tom Brown's Schooldays and The Man Who Bought London, the first film of an Edgar Wallace story, and it closed in 1921.

BGM-CTF.name: The Fellowship Inn
BGM-CTF.text: Your train passes near the Fellowship Inn, on the train's {side}, built in 1923 and 1924 as the first pub on a London housing estate. Fleetwood Mac played there, and the boxer Henry Cooper trained and lived there before his 1963 fight against Cassius Clay.

CFT-CTF.name: Catford Stadium
CFT-CTF.text: Your train passes near the site of Catford Stadium, on the train's {side}, a greyhound track built in 1932 on Southern Railway land between two commuter lines. At its first meeting, on July 30th 1932, the greyhound Mick the Miller was paraded round the track.

CFT-NHD.name: Brockley Jack Theatre
CFT-NHD.text: Your train passes near the Brockley Jack Theatre, on the train's {side}, which shares a building with the Brockley Jack pub. It opened in 1992 with two Chekhov pieces, On the Harmful Effects of Tobacco and Swansong, and puts on new writing as well as established works.

BMS-SRT.name: Simpson's Manor
BMS-SRT.text: Your train passes near the site of Simpson's Place, on the train's {side}, a moated medieval manor house; in the reign of Henry V, William Clark asked for a licence to build it with crenellated walls and a deep moat. It was demolished around 1870, and its name lives on in Simpsons Road.

BKL-BMS.name: St Blaise's Well
BKL-BMS.text: Your train passes near St Blaise's Well, on the train's {side}, a holy well in the grounds of the old palace of the Bishops of Rochester, now part of Bromley Civic Centre. Its water, with traces of iron, was believed to heal, and it became a place of pilgrimage with an oratory to St Blaise beside it.

BKL-SMY.name: Chislehurst Junction
BKL-SMY.text: Your train passes near Chislehurst Junction, on the train's {side}, where the South Eastern and Chatham main lines pass over each other. Loops joining them were built after the two railway companies merged in 1899; the first, the down Bickley Loop, opened on September 8th 1902.

EAL-WEA.name: Pitzhanger Manor
EAL-WEA.text: Your train passes near Pitzhanger Manor, on the train's {side}, the country house that the architect Sir John Soane designed and built for himself between 1800 and 1804.

HAN-WEA.name: Kensington and Chelsea Cemetery, Hanwell
HAN-WEA.text: Your train passes near the Kensington and Chelsea cemetery in Hanwell, on the train's {side}, opened in 1855. One of its tombs, for the shell expert Edgar Smith, is decorated with a large conch shell.
